Who is the present warden?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Creighton.

How long has he been
warden?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He has been in the penitentiary service for a number of years. He was at one time warden's clerk in one of the

penitentiaries, and was afterwards at the head office here for a number of years in the capacity of chief accountant. From time to time he acted as acting warden at different penitentiaries. He was appointed warden of Kingston about two years ago.
What became of the warden who was transferred from Edmonton?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Col. Irving was transferred from Stony Mountain to the warden-ship of Kingston penitentiary, but he has since died.
Did he die as warden, or was he superannuated before his death?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He was superannuated
very shortly before his death.
Is Inspector Hughes serving in the overseas forces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, he is serving at
the front, and is in the trenches at the present time. .
Is he drawing his salary as inspector?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is drawing his salary under the provision of the Order in Council which governed civil servants who enlisted at that time.	[DOT]
What office does he hold in the militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is a Lieutenant-Colonel.
So he draws double pay as colonel and inspector?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hfe draws double pay under the Order in Council which was passed. I may say that that involves no additional expense to the country, because we have managed, at considerable inconvenience to some of the other officials, to get -along without replacing Colonel Hughes in the position of inspector. Though he draws two salaries, the country pays no more money than if some one else had been appointed to the position of colonel. In any event, he draws the two salaries under a general Order in Council which was passed at the outset of the war, and under which civil servants, to whom permission - was given to volunteer, were allowed to retain their salaries.
He draws a salary which another lieutenant-colonel would have drawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It may be an injustice to some other lieutenant-colonel, but it is not costing the country any more money.
Has there been a general decrease in the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I cannot say that there has been a decrease in the staff, but there has been an increase in our convict population.

I thought that since the new prison farm was established in Ontario the judges were more prone to give shorter sentences in order that prisoners might go on the prison farm. I was under the impression that the convicts in our penitentiaries had largely decreased since the establishment of the prison farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether the judges are imposing shorter sentences, but it would appear that more prisoners are being sentenced to long terms, because the convict population of our penitentiaries has increased.
What is the total population of the penitentiaries now, compared with what it was three or four years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the actual number of convicts, when the last report was made, was 2,064. Last year, I believe, the total was 2,008 or 2,009. The increase is not very great.
Has the cost of maintenance increased relatively .compared with what it was three or four years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: During the last two years the cost of maintenance has been the same. The amount we are asking for this year is the same as we asked for last year.
How many convicts have been released from the penitentiaries, since the war began, to sefve in the army, and how many have been recommitted to the penitentiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot give the exact figures; I do not. have them with me; but I am safe in saying that the numbe^ was well under 100. As to re-incarcerations, I cannot speak from memory. There were a few instances, very few, but I will get the exact number.
I suppose that most oi those men who were allowed to enlist were short-term men?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Generally speaking, 1 think that would be correct, but I would

not like to speak positively, as I have not the papers before me. I may say that further reflection upon the whole question, and upon the views of certain military authorities, led us to the conclusion that such releases should be exceedingly rare. I should say that during the past year there have been probably not more than four or five cases. The bulk of them were at the early stage of the war.

Speaking for myself only, and not as a military man in any sense of the word, I would like to congratulate the minister on the change of view, and the change of action, in regard to this matter of the release of prisoners to enable them to undertake military service. I am unable personally to appreciate the advisability of any such action being taken. It is to be presumed that the man who is suffering sentence in a penitentiary is suffering justly for having committed some offence against the well-being of his fellow citizens. After he has been released from the punishment which the law has seen fit to give him, should be time enough to take up the question of accepting his service in aid of the country. It seems to me that the idea of releasing a man from gaol in order that he may enter upon military service indicates a lack of appreciation of the nature, character and importance of the military service that is to be rendered, and of the fact that the man who is rendering military service to his country, under the present circumstances, is not of the less reputable type of citizen, but of the highest type of citizen; the higher the type the better the service. To have it understood that convicted criminals are accepted as volunteers, that they can get immunity for their offences and can be placed in the same position as men who are of the highest and best character and are serving their country from the highest of motives, derogates from the standing and character of the service being rendered by those who are entering under ordinary circumstances. Had not the minister announced that he had reconsidered the original position, I would have desired to enter my most emphatic protest against such action by the Government; and, having heard his expression as to the present policy, I wish to endorse that policy. Of course, it must be admitted that there are exceptional cases which may very well be considered; but to adopt any broad and wholesale policy of that kind would be detrimental to the best interests of the military services as well as to the enforcement of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There never was any
wholesale policy in reference to that. My impression is that up to the first of January, 1915, or in the first six or eight months of the war, there were between 60 and 70 of such enlistments. In dealing with these applications discrimination was made. It never was a matter of wholesale policy. In the great majority of cases there were other reasons, such as the length of time the men had served, good conduct, the recommendation of the warden or judge, and such ordinary reasons as would probably have led to a ticket of leave if they had not come forward and offered to undergo this further condition. However, the further this thing advanced the more impressed were we with the idea and which resulted largely from the expressions of opinion of military authorities, to which all deference should be paid, that the release of a prisoner under these circumstances should be a very exceptional occurrence. It will be realized, I think, that you may have a young man specially fitted, who has had training in military affairs, and who has been led into committing some offence which has brought about the punishment of imprisonment, which offence is manifestly his one, solitary slip, and in regard to. whom there is reason to believe that his future conduct will be irreproachable. In a case of that kind it will be fairly recognized that his patriotic willingness to risk his life in the service of his country may perhaps carry some weight in consideration of whether he ought to be released. However, within the last year, the number of cases has been inside half a dozen.
Is the ticket-of-leave system still in operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it is in very active operation. We have from 25 to 30 applications a day.
What is the general policy followed in connection with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, nobody can lay down absolute rules. There are many circumstances that have to be taken into consideration in determining the advice to be given. In the first place, the nature of the offence is an important factor, as is also the period of time that a man has served when his application comes before us for consideration. There are also the reports and recommendations of the judges, which are always asked for, and which carry very great weight. There is also the report of the warden of the peni-

tentiary, or the offic ,r in charge of the prison, as to the conduct of the prisoner and as to what judgment can be formed from that conduct as to the probable future conduct of the prisoner should he be released. We endeavour to take all these things into consideration, as well as such circumstances as come before us upon the authority of credible people; and to exercise the best judgment we can. Our recommendations can hardly be at fault to any great extent, if we judge by the percentage of men granted tickets-of-leave and who forfeit them by subsequent offences during the period of time which their sentences have still to run. A person granted a ticket of leave is not absolutely absolved from his sentence. He has to report at stated periods, and, if he is convicted of an offence within the balance of the time of his original sentence, he is liable to forfeit his ticket of leave and to be returned to the penitentiary to serve his sentence. The percentage of persons to whom that happens is very small. I think it is under five per cent.
What do you do with a man on a ticket of leave who leaves the country temporarily [DOT] and returns?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The holder of a ticket of leave has no right to leave the country. He is under obligation to report promptly and to remain within the country. If he leaves in violation of that undertaking and comes back, he is liable to find his ticket-of-leave .forfeited and to be returned to the jail from which he was leleased.
I saw a statement to the effect that that branch of the work of the department is now under the Solicitor General.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Solicitor General
does deal with these cases. Of course, they have all to come before the minister ultimately for signature. They go first to an officer of the department, then to the Solicitor General, and finally come to the minister.
I see there is a reduction of $1,000 at St. Vincent de Paul and of $15,000 at the British Columbia penitentiary. You are not putting up certain buildings this year and not contemplating certain work?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At St. Vincent de Paul we are carrying on certain building operations. Last year we voted the amount necessary to complete these operations, they are

about being completed now, and we foresee that $1,000 less than we asked for will be sufficient. As regards the $15,000 reduction in British Columbia, that amount has been dropped because certain pavements in front of the property of the penitentiary which we had purposed constructing in order to place the property in the same position as other properties, we not being taxable, are not now being laid.

Will insane women convicts condemned in the province of Quebec still be taken to Kingston?
_ Mr. DOHERTY: I understand there are at present no women convicts from Quebec. But they are sent to Kingston if there are any. We have adopted the policy of gathering the women convicts together at Kingston. Insane convicts are no longer kept at Kingston. We have done away with the insane ward at Kingston, and insane convicts are distributed amongst the asylums in the different provinces. Those in the province of Quebect are sent to St. Jean de Dieu and Beauport.

Even those under life
terms?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I notice the salaries paid 'to the various surgeons at the penitentiaries have been $1,700, excepting at Kingston, where it has 'been $2,700. Am I right in stating that the reason why an additional $1,000 was given to the surgeon of Kingston penitentiary was that Kingston penitentiary was the place to which all insane convicts from the various provinces were sent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.
I understand that the insane convicts were removed from Kingston penitentiary last June.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On the 14th of July.

If this additional $1,000 was received because of the insane patients at Kingston, and it was not received by the surgeon of any other penitentiary, one would naturally have supposed that the salary would be discontinued when the insane patients were removed from Kingston; but, notwithstanding their removal, I am informed that the surgeon at Kingston penitentiary continued to draw the same salary up to the end of 1915. That strikes me as needing explanation, which I have no doubt the minister can give.
Are the surgeons permitted to carry on outside practice?

No, up t-o the end of last year they were not, but I believe a different arrangement has been made in regard to Kingston penitentiary. Another observation I was going to make was that while the salary of the various penitentiary surgeons, with the exception of the one at Kingston, is $1,700, the number of convicts in the different institutions varies very greatly. For instance, for the year ending March 21,	1914, which is the last
report available, Kingston had 511; St. Vincent de Paul, 401; Saskatchewan, 108; Alberta, 203; British Columbia, 379; Manitoba, 172, and Dorchester, 231. I think the system in regard to the penitentiary surgeons has been entirely wrong. The surgeons should not be prevented from practising their profession outside of the time required for their duties in connection with the penitentiary. A good move has been made at Kingston penitentiary in replacing the former surgeon by two physicians; not only do I think it was a good move to provide two surgeons instead of one, but it was a good move to replace the former surgeon anyway, for he clearly showed his unfitness and incompetence while he was occupying the office. Generally speaking, I think it is a step in the right direction to have two physicians attached to these institutions, particularly the larger ones like Kingston and St. Vincent de Paul. I think also that the surgeons should be allowed to practise their profession outside of the time required for their duties at the penitentiary. There are many reasons for that. With two physicians, each has the advantage of consultation with the other. Again, when an operation has to be performed, at least two surgeons are required, and they would then be officials of the institution; and there are many other reasons which might be mentioned. The minister has seen fit to make the change and appoint two physicians at Kingston. It is ia good move, which I think should be followed in all the other institutions throughout the country. The salaries of penitentiary surgeons might reasonably, perhaps, be cut down in some of the smaller institutions, and I have no doubt the surgeons would be willing to accept a reduction if they were allowed to follow their profession outside. That is all I wish to say on that particular phase of the penitentiaary problem. I should like
an explanation from the minister why Dr. Phelan's salary was continued for the balance of 1915, if the insane convicts had been removed in July.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the hon. member
has said, the insane patients were removed from the insane ward, which was abolished, and placed in the different insane asylums on July 14, 1915. That, of course, brought about a situation which in effect abolished the office held by Dr. Phelan, so far as that office consisted in the superintendency oi the penitentiary, for which an allowance of $1,000 was made. That would 4 p.m. have left intact his position as surgeon to the penitentiary, to which was attached a salary of $1,700; but at that time, in addition to the abolition oi his position of superintendent, it was thought advisable to adopt the new system which the hon. member has mentioned with .regard to surgeons, and which I am very happy to know meets with his approval; that is to say, instead of a surgeon being bound to give his entire time to the service of the penitentiary and receiving a salary of $1,700, it was decided, as was permitted to us under the statute, to allow the gentleman whom we should retain as surgeon to the penitentiary to carry on a general practice, and to reduce his salary by twenty per cent. That change, involving the abolition of the position to which Dr. Phelan had been appointed, and had held for a great many years, we found ourselves in the position where, as the office as a whole was about to be abolished, Dr. Phelan's services to the institution would cease. Under these circumstances, as has been usual with regard to persons who have held office for a long period of time and have reached a certain age, Dr. Phelan, previous to his ceasing to perform his functions, was given three months' leave of absence. As an actual fact, I think the patients left on the 14th of July, and Dr. Phelan's leave ran from the 25th of July to the 25th of October. It had been anticipated that during that interval the change with regard to the employment of a physician or surgeon would have been made and Dr. Phelan replaced. The matter of selection of physicians, not merely from the point of view of the person to be appointed to replace Dr. Phelan, but also from the point of view of the system to be adopted, called for some consideration. I felt that there was room for improvement in the system that had prevailed. I had before me a suggestion of the Investigating

Commission, that I should appoint a resident physician, which, as I understand it, is some one to live within the building, and a visiting physician. I had also before me another suggestion which I thought, and still think, had a great deal of merit, though it was not finally acted upon; and that was that I should have three doctors acting in consultation. All these suggestions called for consideration, and the selection of persons to fill the positions was a matter that I felt should be carefully dealt with. The result was that when Dr. Phelan's leave of absence expired his position had not been filled. We were expecting to fill it, and to bring the matter to a close, day after day. His engagement therefore ran on, and when it was terminated the position was dealt with as one position; and, of *course, if we were right 'hi granting the leave of absence it would apply to him as holding an office with these two branches which was being termin.afd. For the sub- [DOT] sequent period, from' the 25th October until the end of December, there was delay in .filling the position, so far as that ef physician is concerned, and during that delay it had not seemed desirable that we should do. otherwise than avail ourselves of the services of Dr. Phelan as physician and surgeon to the establishment. The result was that the whole matter was dealt with in December-I have forgotten the exact date of the Order in 'Council, but it was made to take effect on December 31. I may say that it was by inadvertence of my own that Dr. Phelan .received, after the expiry of his leave of absence for a couple of months, the salary attaching to his position as superintendent of the insane ward. But it did occur to me that it was not a proper thing that he should be paid for the duties of an office that had expired. However, if he was not to have his salary to the end of the year, he was certainly entitled to his superannuation allowance under the statute. I looked into the question and found that for the period between the expiry of his leave of absence on the 25th October, and the final termination of his holding of office as surgeon the differ. ence between paying him his salary and paying him the superannuation allowance to which he was entitled would come to $80 and some odd cents. 1 found that, although the position of superintendent of the 'insane ward had been abolished, Dr. Phelan had, in that period, rendered us service which would otherwise have-been rendered by a physician 
specially employed, one competent to deal with insqne patients. For instance we had occasion to examine at the St. Jean de Dieu asylum a patient concerning whose insanity a difference of opinion had arisen. This man, iGodbout, had been sent to St. Jean de Dieu, to which institution the insane are sent who are sentenced from the district of Montreal; but the doctors there questioned his insanity. Dr. iPhelan made the examination. In addition, there was a convict, Martinuk, who had been sentenced to death, but whose sentence had been commuted on a question of insanity, and it was necessary to have his condition determined within three months of his going into the asylum, in order to entitle this Government to return him to the care of the Provincial Government should he be found insane. Dr. Phelan made that examination and report. He also dealt with the convict Bonner, who was transferred as insane to the Guelph infirmary. Further, he made an examination of Percy Scott, a prisoner in the Manitoba penitentiary, under sentence of death. In view of these services having been rendered, and in view of the difference involved as between paying the salary, or paying the retiring allowance, it seemed to me that that difference certainly was not an exaggerated remuneration for the services Tendered by Dr. Phelan during that period. The hon. gentleman will realize that if we had employed an outside physician to render these services the cost to us would have been very much more than that sum.
As regards the suggestion of our extending the change in the manner of employing the physicians to the penitentiaries generally, I am quite prepared to say that that represents my own view of the subject But I thought it wise, as we were making the change at Kingston, to wait a little and see whether it worked out as satisfactorily as I have every reason to anticipate it will, before making it of general applica-t.on. There is another consideration that arises with regard to the question of having a gentleman as surgeon who will give Ins entire time, as compared with having one take a smaller salary, trusting to outside practice, and that is the consideration of the locality of the penitentiary. At Kingston, and at some other places, the plan can readily be carried out, because we have at our door a city where a physician who gives part of 'his time to our institution will find fair opportunity-I think excellent op-

portunity-for general practice. But when you come to deal with the penitentiary at St. Vincent de Paul, a small village, or the penitentiary at' Dorchester, which is in the same position, or the penitentiary at Stoney Mountain, which is a certain distance from Winnipeg, it is more difficult to find a gentleman willing to give us only a part of hie time, and certainly it will not be easy to find two gentlemen willing to engage at the present small salary. If we find that we can make satisfactory arrangements at these penitentiaries, I shall be very glad to extend the system. With regard to the remark about the similarity of salaries in all the penitentiaries without regard to the number of patients, there is no doubt that there is an anomaly there. The salaries, however, are fixed by the statute. It is not impossible that when the statute was enacted it might have been well if consideration had been given to the fact that a different quantum of service is called for in the different penitentiaries. Over against that was this:	the system was
adopted of making all the salaries identical in all the penitentiaries, because it was thought wise that we should not attach a man in any permanent way to one institution; that we should have the officers all at our disposal, so that a man could be transferred if it was found that he could be more useful in another penitentiary than that in which he was employed. There would be great difficulty in carrying that out if the salaries were different in the different institutions. I am prepared to concede that that consideration is not of as direct application to the surgeons as it is to the regular disciplinary officers of the institution. I am not prepared to say that if thought had been given at the time the salaries were fixed to the difference between the professional gentlemen who attend the penitentiaries and those who are properly called the officers of the penitentiaries, it might not have been wise to make a difference in the salaries at the different institutions, based in some way upon the relative amount of work to be done at each.

(Translation.) Mt. Chairman, I see by the report of the inspector of penitentiaries for the fiscal year ending the 31st of March, 1914, of the Inspector of Penitentiaries for the cost of maintenance per convict is quite high. At Kingston, the cost per head is $313.48; at St. Vincent de Paul, $392.21; at Dorchester, $430.98; in Manitoba, $411.85; in British Columbia, $.350.02; for Alberta, $472.33, while for Saskatchewan it goes up to
$961.75. As my hon. friend, the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver)-who I notice is not in his seat just now-is preaching economy, I think he might suggest the means of diminishing the cost of the maintenance of convicts in his province, because it comes to about double what obtains elsewhere under like conditions.
In going over the items for maintenance, it seems to me that the excessive cost is due in, the main to the wages paid to the staff of the penitentiary. It is possible that such a condition of things was merely temporary, but I am not aware of that as I have not seen the report of the inspector for 1915. But in 1914, the difference in the cost as compared with the expenditure in other penitentiaries, is so great as to call for an explanation.
As my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) whom I now see in his seat, is always anxious to promote the best interests of the French-Canadians, I should like to ask him a favour for the province of Ontario; I should like him to ask the Government or suggest to his friends, the appointment of a few more French-speaking employees at the Kingston penitentiary. In looking over the staff, I find only one French name out of a list of 96 employees. Not that I care to see more of my people appointed in penitentiaries rather than elsewhere; but as a matter of public convenience, the French-speaking people of Ontario amount to one-twelfth, and there must unfortunately be in the penitentiary some French-speaking convicts, who would welcome among the officers some that could understand them. I know -that among -the French element in Ontario, chiefly in the east, there are a certain number who do not understand the English language. Should any of them be incarcerated-it is painful enough for them to have to undergo a sentence-their fate could be somewhat alleviated by those employees who could speak to them in their own language. I believe we have there a serious grievance not only as to the French-Canadians of Ontario but with respect to French convicts from other provinces. I therefore appeal to our friends from Ontario to deal more fairly with the French-Canadians in that respect.
I now desire to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to another point. While going through the Dorchester penitentiary, in New Brunswick, I found there yount; men 12 or 15 years of age interned with oldeT criminals. I called it to the attention of

the officer who was seeing me through the institution. I think he told me that there were no reformatories for younger delinquents in New Brunswick. Here is ample room for improvement and I call the minister's especial notice to it. I think it is not in the interest of'.morality well conceived, to place juvenile offenders with older convicts. If the Government has power to do it, some means ought to foe found of taking those young men out of the penitentiary and confining them in other special institutions where they would get a chance of reforming. In the penitentiaries, they come Unto contact with older cr.minals, and there is a greater opportunity for them of getting lost completely instead of reforming.
At Dorchester also, I noticed that there was no one to understand French, I would have liked to obtain more information, but I could not get them to understand me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
(Translation.) For the hon. member's information as to the relative oo<st of the maintenance of convicts in Saskatchewan, as compared with the other provinces, I will ask him to consider one point which probably has escaped his attention. The figures he has mentioned do not represent the cost of maintenance of each particular convict, font are obtained by taking the total expenditure of each institution and dividing it by the number of convicts therein. So that, as the hon. member will readily see, where the number oi convicts is less, the necessary result is a higher cost per head. In every one of those establishments the buildings have to be kept up and the officers and employees paid. It follows that in dividing the total maintenance between four to five hundred convicts, the ratio per head is much smaller than where the number of convicts is much less. No doubt the maintenance of the prisoners in the western provinces, and especially in Saskatchewan, costs higher than elsewhere, but the difference does not lie where the hon. member thinks.
Now, as to the inquiry which the hon. member for Bimouski made to the hon. member for Frontenac, I leave it to the latter to answer for himself.
'My hon. friend from Bimouski has brought to my notice the establishment oi jails, reformatories >and houses of detention for prisoners sentenced to less than two years. The establishment and maintenance of such institutions come within the ex-

elusive jurisdiction, of the provinces. So that I am afraid the Government cannot intervene to redress the grievances he mentions.
Now I am surprised to hear from the hon. gentleman that he had found no one to speak to him in French in the Dorchester penitentiary. I know that I for one appointed some French-speaking employees, and there must be others whose names, at any rate are French^Canadian or Acadian names. It was a misfortune that- none should have happened around when he went through. However, it is far from us to wish to discriminate against the Frenchspeaking people.
(Translation.) Does it happen only in the Maritime Provinces that children from. 12 to 15 years of age are put in penitentiaries?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: (Translation.) I did not understand the member for Bimouski to mention children from 12 to 15 years of age. However, I may say that in certain sections in New Brunswick-I have been informed by some judges that they prefer to send the. young culprits to the penitentiary, because they state, in their opinion, the conditions in some of the jails of the province are such as to make it desirable in the interest of the children themselves. But I do not think there can be found a large number of children as young as that in the penitentiaries. In the different provinces, and I believe in the case of New Brunswick, special houses and reformatories have been established, and I should be very much surprised1 if there existed a more than insignificant number of cases such as were mentioned by the hon. member. At any rate, that does not come within Federal jurisdiction. We have, -according to law, to provide for the' convicts which the courts send us.

(Translation.) Here in Ontario, we have reformatories for boys and for girls, and even for Catholic and for Protestant children. If some of the provinces have not seen fit to build those reformatories, it might be good for this Parliament to amend the Criminal Code so -as to forbid the courts sentencing children to the penitentiary.

The Dorchester penitentiary, while a Dominion institution, is in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and I am therefore interested in anything which refers to the conduct of its

affairs. As I understood the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay), he complains that there are very few if any, Acadians employed in the institution.
I said that while I noticed that on the list of employees about one out of six were French, when I visited the institution I could not find one French employee.

I do not know where the
French employees would be on the day my hon. friend was there, but from the list I notice there are a number of French-speaking people employed. The deputy warden is an Acadian, there is a French chaplain, and there are a number of French guards. I was surprised that my hon. friend was not able to find a French employee when he visited the penitentiary. As to boys being sent to the penitentiary, I am not here to speak in defence of the institution, except as I know it from living within 10 miles of it, and visiting it frequently. I have heard no complaint of that practice. We have a reformatory in St. John to which boys who are convicted of offences are sent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not wish to convey the idea that this is at all general, but there have been instances.

In New Brunswick we have a reformatory. I think they have also some reformatories or boys' schools in Nova Scotia to which boys would be sent, unless there was some special reason for sending them to the penitentiary.

I had an opportunity not long ago of visiting the Dbrchester penitentiary. I addressed myself to the officer in French and I was answered in French. I was taken around the institution, and I had good French conversation at all points. I think if the hon. member for Rimouski had addressed himself first in French he would probably have got the right officer to answer him. I do not mean to say that we have our share of French-speaking employees in that institution, but I am aware that we have many French officers and employees there.	,
As to sending young boys to the penitentiary, a case occurred not long ago where a young boy of sixteen years was sentenced to two years' imprisonment, but the judge sent him to the boys' industrial home, a very good school. As a matter of fact, very few young boys are sent to the penitentiary; they are sent to the boys' industrial home.
On what was the pension of Dr. Phelan based?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The pension was based upon the provisions of the statute in that regard. Dr. Phelan had served some eighteen years. When he came into the service he was more than thirty years of age, and, coming in as a physician and taking a position where special professional qualifications were required^ he came under section 12 of the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement Act. Furthermore, Dr. Phelan's connection with the institution was terminated by the abolition of the office which he held. He therefore came under section 15 of the same Act. Each of these sections provides that in any case where a man comes under the conditions prescribed by it, and, as I said, he came under those prescribed by both sections-ten years may be added to the number of years actually served, in estimating his superannuation. In the case of Dr. Phelan, both the provisions of the statute being applicable, they were acted upon, and his superannuation allowance was fixed accordingly.

I desire to enter my protest against the course which has been taken by the Department of Justice in connection with this matter, and I shall endeavour to give some reasons why I enter that protest. Dr. Phelan was appointed in 1897. He received a salary of $2,700 a year, $1,000 of which was given to him in consideration of the fact that he had under his care the insane convicts sent' from various parts of Canada to Kingston peni-tentiry. These insane convicts were removed from that institution, I think, in July, but Dr. Phelan still continued to draw his share of the $1,000 to the end( of the year. The Minister of Justice has given his explanation of that. On the retirement of Dr. Phelan, at the end of 1915, two men were appointed in his place. The minister will agree with me-in fact, he has said so-that the appointment of the two men is an improvement. I have nothing to say in regard to the capabilities of the two men who have been appointed; I am personally acquainted with both of them. They are very estimable men and rank high in the profession. I think I am safe in saying that Dr. Hanley ranks as high in hi* profession as Dr. Phelan ever did. Dr. W. T. Connell is noted from one end of Canada to the other, I might almost say from one end of this continent to the other,

as a specialist along bacteriological lines. Dr. Hanley receives for his services $860 a year, and Dr. Connell receives as consulting physician $500 a year. The sum of $1,360 is being paid to these two men for looking after the welfare of the convicts in Kingston penitentiary, and Dr. Phelan is drawing an annuity of $1,512 a year for the rest of his life. He had served, as I say, for 18 years. Ten years were added to his service, and his annuity was brought up by that means to the sum of $1,500. I think I am right in saying that out of the 45 men in the various departments of the Civil Service of the Dominion who were retired last year, because of age, or for some equally good and sufficient reason, the only man who had anything added to his service was Dr. Phelan, the surgeon of Kingston penitentiary.
I want to state some reasons why I do not think Dr. Phelan was entitled to receive this special consideration at the hands of the Department of Justice. In the course of the investigation which was held at Kingston it was proved that Dr. Phelan used violent and filthy language to a guard of the institution in the presence of others. His language on that occasion was so filthy that no paper would print it, and no person would be allowed to make use of it in any public gathering. The proof that he did use this indecent language is to be found on page 389 of the typewritten evidence taken before the commission. I find it necessary to give the page of that evidence, because, for some reason or other, when making out their brief report, for which they received pretty nearly $5,000, the commissioners refer you to page blank when you want to corroborate their statements by the evidence. This occurs in fifty or sixty places. Throughout their report they have left out the page of the typewritten evidence so that the report is of no use whatever for the purpose of reference. You cannot use the report without looking up the evidence. Why that was done is a mystery to me. It certainly made it impossible for the members of this House, if they desired to look into the question thoroughly and to form an estimate of this report from the evidence which was produced before the commission, to get any guidance from the evidence.
I make the statement that it was proved conclusively, and admitted, the proof of which is found on page 389 of the typewritten evidence, that Dr. Phelan, the man who has been superannuated with $1,500 a year, made use of language that was too

foul for the lowest kind of man to use. The very fact that a man of his standing, and of his profession, would so far forget himself as to make use of language of that stamp, shows that he is not the sort of man who is entitled to special consideration at the hands of this Government. It was also proven in the course of the evidence-taken by the commission, the proof of 'which you will find, if you care to take the trouble to look it up, on page 421 ot the typewritten evidence, that Dr. Phelan tried to induce one of the guards, who was giving evidence before the commission, to commit perjury.
When was the investigation held?

About a year and a half ago. Is a man who had been an officer of the Goyernment for 18 years, and who, when a commission is appointed to investigate, goes so far as to try to get one of the witnesses before that commission to commit perjury, the sort of man to have ten years added to his service and to be pensioned off at $1,500 a year?
It was also proven before that investigating commission that Dr. Phelan played the part of a petty grafter. There is no question at all about that. He admitted that he had grafted small amounts, that he had taken as fees small amounts from men who were seeking positions as guards. He admitted also that he was not entitled to do so. I think he showed the same disposition in the latter half of 1915 when he continued to draw cheques as physician of an insane ward which did not exist. The very first rule laid down for the guidance of the surgeon of Kingston penitentiary or of any other penitentiary, is rule 52. Will the fninister or anyone	else	say that	Dr.Phelan ever attempted to live up to that rule, or	to	give	effect to	it?The same may	be	said	in regard	torule 53, which deals with the hygiene and cleanliness of the prison; that rule was disregarded	by	him.	The evidence
shows that 60 or 70 convicts used the same cup in drinking water; that some of the convicts had loathsome diseases, and that there were men, actually with syphilitic sores in their mouths, who were using the cup to get drinking water, other convicts being obliged to use the same cup or go without any water. It was Phelan's place to see that that condition of affairs did not exist; yet it did exist, and the fact was brought out clearly in the evidence.

In the course of the inquiry Dr. Young was called in as a specialist. Dr. Young had been connected with Portsmouth Insane Asylum for years, and on page 10 of the commissioner's report we find Dr. Young using these words with reference to the prison patients under the care of the prison surgeon:
. The physical condition of the patients shows the effect of improper diet, insufficient exercise, and fresh air.
Yet Dr. Phelan, in his report to Ottawa year after year, stated that the sanitary conditions, and everything else about the prison and the insane ward in the hospital were as perfect as it was possible for human beings to make them. That is the way he reported year after year; the minister's own report will show that very clearly. And yet Dr. Young, when called in, says that the patients show the ill effects of improper diet, insufficient exercise, and lack of fresh air. The former warden of the prison, Dr. Platt, said the medical superintendent, who was prison surgeon, makes a short call, Sundays expected, and that this constitutes the whole care and treatment of the criminal insane. The commissioners, in face of Dr. Young's statement, made this statement, which will be found on page 11 of their report:
Many an unfortunate must, have been deprived of a fair chance of recovery by reason of the State's unpardonable neglect.
That is to say, by reason of the unpardonable neglect of the prison surgeon, as the report shows clearly, the sanitation was imperfect, the diet was imperfect, and the patients lacked for proper food and care. The commissioners went on to say:
Further, we find that Insane inmates have not received the attention which their state demanded and in some instances they have been subjected to unjustifiable punishments.
Not only did Dr. Phelan not visit the sick convicts on Sundays, but he reported everything as good as it was possible to be while these sick convicts, in order to allow the guards to go home, were actually given their breakfast at 9 o'clock in the morning, their dinner at 11 o'clock in the morning, their supper at 1 p.m., and they got nothing after that until next morning. That was under the direct supervision of the prison surgeon who is singled out for special favour in regard to a pension.
This gentleman is on record, proven clearly by the evidence, as having used foul and indecent language which certainly a man of his profession should not have used. It
certainly marked him as an inferior man. He is proven clearly by the records to have resorted to petty grafting. It is also proven by the records that he had endeavoured to get one of the witnesses before the commission to commit perjury. The records show that he neglected to care for the sick patients, while his report year after year was a gross misrepresentation of the conditions as they existed at Kingston penitentiary. Carlyle says:
(Show me the man you honour; I know by that symptom better than any other what kind of man you are yourself, for, you show me what your ideal of manhood is, what kind of a man you long to be.
I would be sorry to think for one moment that the Minister of Justice would be measured by these words, I can only conclude that the Minister of Justice, in giving this man the consideration which he has given him, and which, in my judgment he is not entitled to, has been grossly misled. He has not looked into the facta which have been brought out by the commission, and because of that he has been more generous to this man than this man's record would warrant him in being.
I have here a report signed by Douglas Stewart and W. S. Hughes, who occupy the positions of inspectors of penitentiaries. I think every person will agree with me in this, that if Douglas Stewart and W. S. Hughes, inspectors of penitentiaries, feel that they are entitled in their report to speak freely in regard to the action of others, others have the right to speak freely in regard to them. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that in so far as that report is concerned, the report for the year ended March 31, 1914, Douglas Stewart and W. S.
Hughes, inspectors of pem-5 p.m. tentiaries, make statements which, it seems to me, they must know are false and misleading to the public and the members of this House who take the trouble to read their report. Let me refer to one or two of the statements which they make. These two inspectors in this report take very strong exception to the criticism .of the way in which Kingston penitentiary was conducted. They seem to think that no person has the right to interfere, or to call attention to wrongdoing in connection with this institution, because of their connection with it as officials. They find fault with the persons who make charges. They state that these charges are false. Well, I may say that one of the men who signs this report as

inspector, and who, in signing the report says that the statements and allegations made in regard to the administration of this penitentiary are false and misleading, is the very man who 'is responsible for nine-tenths of the statements which were made in regard to that institution. I am referring to W. S. Hughes, who before he became inspector of penitentiaries, and drew the -salary which he is getting in that position, was a very different man. W. S. Hughes, while he was accountant of the Kingston penitentiary, and drew $1,500 or $1,700 -a year as salary, was wonderfully outspoken. He charged pretty nearly every crime in the category against other officials of the institution. But when W. S. Hughes began to draw the salary of an inspector of penitentiaries a sudden change canfe over the spirit of his dream. He had no sooner landed that position than he declared that he would not go on the stand and tell all he knew in regard to the Kingston penitentiary and the wrong-doing there. I asked him why, and his reply to me was that every tub must stand on its bottom.
Had the commission no power to compel -him to answer questions?

Yes, I suppose they had, and I have no hesitation in saying that a proper commission would have done so. What I have stated here, and what I state now, is that that commission, with the men who were appointed to act upon it, was an absolute farce. I repeat what I have said on a former occasion, that from the standpoint of the proper conduct of the duties of commissioners they were not worth fifteen cents a day, and that would be a high price to pay for their services.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to- say that, before the commission Inspector Hughes was asked questions and that he refused to answer them, or is he speaking of something which occurred outside?

I state in regard to Inspector Hughes that, before the commission was appointed, the inspector made a number of allegations and charges in regard to the institution. He made them not only verbally, but in writing, and I have them in my possession. That is about the strongest proof I can give of my statements. He was not at all backward in making these statements, and I can frankly say now, as I have said before, that it was 
because of the statements made by Inspector Hughes, and because I found on inquiry that many of these statements were true and could be corroborated, that I asked for an investigation into the conduct of this institution. I say also that after the investigation was started, after Inspector Hughes had been appointed as inspector, and after he had been summoned to appear before the commission, he telegraphed to me on what train he was coming to Kingston. I went down to meet him. The statement he made to me was that, in view of the fact that the Minister of Justice had, in his judgment, very wrongly put a time limit of five	years upon the investigation, if he were in my position he would throw up the sponge and have nothing more to do with it. I told Inspector Hughes that I was not built along those lines; that I never started anything unless I felt that I should start it, and that when I started I did not quit. He told me then that, because he was an inspector, he would not go on the witness stand and tell all he knew in regard to the mismanagement of the Kingston penitentiary. He went on the stand and took the usual oath to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, although he had stated to me but a short time before that he had no intention of telling the whole truth. That is what I say in regard to Inspector Hughes. And I say further, that I believe this sudden change which came over him is- to be attributed to the dollars which he received in the position he now occupies as compared with the salary he got in his former position. It -has been hinted that there were other reasons; as, for instance, that those against whom h-e would have made charges had certain charges up their sleeves ready to throw at him.
What were the names of the commissioners?

G. M. Macdonell, Dr. Etherington, and J. P. Downey, the two former from Kingston and the latter from Orillia. In the course of their report the inspectors state that they have sought to avoid extremes in dealing with the prisoners :
Brutality and coddling have been avoided as equally dangerous ; the former because it incites revenge against society, and the latter because It invites criminality by making the way of the trangressor easy.
I shall have a word to say in regard to brutality in a moment. With regard to cod-

dling, if the inspectors are not aware, they should be aware how prisoners in that institution are treated. I make the statement that there is gross discrimination. For instance, Travers, who wrecked the Farmers' Bank, was not treated the same as the other prisoners. He was given as good food as any person would get outside; he was allowed cigars and his pipe; and when he went to Toronto, in the custody of one of the officers of the institution, to give evidence before Justice Meredith in the Farmers' Bank investigation, he found an opportunity to order some liquor to be sent down. I do not know to whom the liquor was *shipped, but I do know that he gave the order when he was supposed to be in the custody of one of the guards. I do know that while he was an inmate of the institution he was allowed privileges which the other convicts were not allowed. He was allowed food which the other convicts were not allowed, and he was allowed tobacco which the other convicts were not allowed. The inspectors should have known that, if the officers of the institution are letting them know the goings-on as they should. Further on in their report the inspectors state:	.
The commission fails to disclose a single case of cruelty, inhumanity, or wilful injustice to any convict substantiated by evidence that would be accepted as such in any police court in the country.
And further:
No prison punishment can be inflicted except on the authority of the warden. No punishment was ever authorized or ever was inflicted on an inmate of the insane ward, although false statements to that effect have been made and published.
I say that that statement of the inspectors is absolutely untrue, and I am in a position, I think, to prove to the satisfaction of the committee that it is untrue. It is true that the commissioners saw fit to call a great many convicts to give evidence. In connection with the charges I made before the commsision I did not have any convict called, but relied entirely for substantiation of those charges upon such evidence as might be adduced from the officials of the institution. So, as regards the calling of convicts to give evidence, that was up to the commission entirely, and in that matter I certainly think they acted very peculiarly.
Let me give an instance, and this will appeal particularly to the lawyers in the House. A certain man named Rose, serving a life sentence at Kingston, was brought before the commission to give evidence in
connection with the charges made against one of the officials

not a charge made by myself. The next day after giving his evidence, Rose asked to see the warden and myself. The warden, Col. Irvine, and I had an interview with Rose, in which he told us that the evidence which he had given against the official the day previous was false. He said he had perjured himself in giving that evidence, and had done so at the instigation of another official. In the presence of Col. Irvine, I called the attention of the Chief Commissioner, Mr. Macdonell, to that fact, thinking that he would recall the man and question him in regard to his evidence of the previous day, which had gone on record. But he refused to recall him, stating that it would be a serious matter if Rose were found guilty of perjury. Personally, I do not see how it could have made matters much worse for Rose, because he was serving a life sentence anyway. I want to call attention, particularly of the lawyers of the committee-and the hon. minister is himself an ex^judge-to this: Although the chief commissioner refused to recall this man and question him in regard to the voluntary statement he made to me and Cbl. Irvine, that the evidence he had given the previous day was perjured, later on actually called this self-confessed perjurer to give evidence before the commission on another matter. I am not a lawyer, but I do not think it requires a legal mind to conclude that a commissioner who had no more idea of proper procedure than that- well, I think it goes a long way towards justifying my statement of a moment ago that he was not worth fifteen cents, let alone the amount he received.
The inspectors state that no prison punishment was inflicted or authorized to. be inflicted on an inmate of the insane ward. In that connection I wish to call the attention of the commission to page 787 of the evidence, where Guard Bryant-this is not convict evidence-who, I believe, is still on the staff of the institution, swore that he did see insane convicts stripped of their clothing, their arms strapped to their sides and their legs strapped together, immersed in ice cold water. ex-Guard Babcock on page 796 of the evidence confirms that statement, and says that he took part in the tubbing of these insane convicts. McWatters was another of the guards who came forward and swore that that sort of thing was going on in the institution. In the face of that how can, or how dare, the inspectors sign this re-

port and make the statement they do here that "no punishment was ever authorized or inflicted on an inmate of the insane ward." And what do the commissioners say in regard to that? I quote from the evidence at page 796:
Q. Ever see a prisoner put in the tub to give him a cold bath?-A. Yes.
Q. Where was that?-A. Asylum,
Q. By whose orders?-A. Mr. McWatters.
Q. What office did he hold?-A. Acting keeper, I think, at the time.
Q. Why was the tubbing done?-A. He insulted another officer.
Q. How did you proceed to punish this man? -A. Filled the tub with water and put him into it.
Q. And held him down?-A. Yes. -
Q. In the cold water?-A. Yes.
Dr. Etherington:	An insane patient?
By Mr. Downey:
Q. How long did they keep him in the cold bath?-A. I could not tell you how long they kept him in. They kept him in till he gave up, till he said he was sorry for what he had done; that is all I know.
By Mr. Stewart:
Q. Was he held under the.water?-A. Yes.
Q. Was he there half an hour?-A. No, he would have been dead if he was.
Q. Was he pushed down in the water?-A. He was.
Q. Was he smothering when he came up?- A. He was.
Q. Did you ever see blood coming out of the mouths and noses of convicts treated in that way?-A. Not out of him.
Q. Did you like that treatment?-A. I would not want it myself.
I say, it has been established beyond any question, by men who are not convicts, by reliable men, men who are still in the institution as officials, that insane convicts were subjected to this tubbing. The inspectors must have had these facts before them; and I do not see how, in the face of that, they could make the statement they do, that no punishment was inflicted on an inmate of the insane ward. Unquestionably that punishment was inflicted again and again; the insane person was stripped, his hands were bound, his feet were tied together, and he was put into cold water just as it came from the tap, whether it was January or July.
The hon. gentleman read a question as put by Mr. Stewart?

That was a lawyer, not the inspector. Now I wish to call attention to another statement made in the report of the inspectors:
The evidence fails to disclose a single case of cruelty or inhumanity.
Well, as to that, I would refer hon. members to page 17 of the report. The com-

missioners were questioning Inspector Douglas Stewart in regard to hosing. This is the conversation that took place:
Q. You And this (hosing) more efficient (than the triangle)?-A. More effective.
Q. What is It that makes it so effective with these convicts?-A. It takes the defiance out of them.
Q. How?-A. If you got the hose you would know.
Q. What is it?-A. I suppose it is the impact of the hose against the body, knocks the wind out of them.
Q. And it seems to succeed where nothing else will?-A. Yes, it never failed yet.
Q. To beat an incorrigible convict into submission?-A. Yes.
And, further on:
Q. Is that the most severe punishment?-A. No. I think shooting is more severe.
Q. You mean killing a man outright?-A. Yes.
Of course, Inspector Stewart is entitled to his opinion, as I am entitled to mine. He thinks it all right to turn the hose on a convict with water at a pressure of sixty or seventy pounds to the inch, as he says it was in St. Vincent de Paul. He thinks it is effective; in fact, according to his own statement, he thinks there is only one thing more effective, and that is to _ shoot the man. He not only thinks it effective, but in his judgment-and I give him credit for being honest in his opinion-it is humane. I take exception to that; I do not think it is humane. I think it shows a very wrong state of affairs when a cell is specially constructed with rounded corners so that the convict cannot escape, the convict is put into this cell and the hose is _ turned on him at a pressure of sixty or seventy pounds to the inch. " The wind is knocked out of him," as one of these witnesses says, and he is knocked about the cell like a football. I say, in my judgment, that is not proper treatment, and no good can result from it. It may be all Tight to use the hose to disperse a mob, but to turn it upon a man in a small cell is not, in my judgment, humane, and I think it does not reflect any credit on the inspectors who say that that is proper treatment, nor upon the officials of the institution where such treatment is permitted. In this, of course,
I am expressing my own opinion, as I have a perfect right to do.
Now, I have one or two questions I wish to ask the Minister of Justice. That hon. gentleman occupies a position of very great, importance in the government of the country; I cannot conceive of a position of greater importance than his. It is a posi-

tion that has been occupied in the past by some very able men. The responsibility rests upon the Minister of Justice of seeing to it that the laws are administered fairly and equitably to all. I am not going to make any charge that they are not so administered, but I am going to call to the attention of the minister one or two things of which I should like an explanation. He may have-I hope he will have-a clear explanation in regard to these points. I called his attention to them on a former occasion in this House. He did not then give any explanation, but I hope he will favour me with an explanation on this occasion.
In 1912 one of the officers of Stoney Mountain penitentiary was caught carrying in or taking out letters, Which is contrary to the regulation. He lost his position because of that act, and was fined, I believe, whatever pay was coming to him at that time. In August, 1914, another official of that institution, the Roman Catholic chaplain, Rev. J. A. Joubert, was caught doing the same thing. The acting warden of that institution telegraphed to Ottawa on August 12 the facts 'concerning the suspension of this gentleman.
His prison order book shows this:
Aug. 12, 1914. Order No. 2. The Rev. J. A. Joubert is suspended from duty as Roman Catholic chaplain until further notice from this date.
(Signed) W. R. Grahame, Deputy Warden.
Subsequently he received a telegram from the minister which led him to make this entry in the book on August 13, 1914, as order No. 3:
The suspension of the Roman Catholic chaplain is withdrawn to conform with the wishes of the Minister of Justice.
(Signed) W. R. Grahame,
Deputy Warden.
I hope that the minister has a clear explanation with regard to this matter. It is a matter of indifference to me who acts as chaplain of that institution, but I want to point out that an immense responsibility rests on the head of the Department of Justice. It is important that the people of the country should not think, rightly or wrongly, that the same standard of justice is not accorded to all. I do not say that there are two standards; I am simply calling these facts to the attention of the minister in the hope that he will give an explanation which will satisfy the public that there was a good and substantial reason
134	'
fox treating one man differently from the way another was treated.
At the time the investigation was held in Kingston it became apparent to the commissioners that certain officials were accepting money from the friends of convicts; that they kept some of this money as a sort of percentage or commission, and handed the rest to the convicts. When, the commissioners became convinced that something of that kind was going on, they issued a sort of proclamation in which they stated that while the act was a criminal one, if any guards who had been guilty of these acts would come forward and confess their fault, they would lose their positions, but no criminal action would be taken against them. Two guards did come forward and admit that they had been trafficking in that way; accordingly, as was quite proper, they lost their positions. In looking for evidence in regard to this matter, the records of the post office were searched, and it was found that three money orders had been cashed by Rev. Mr. McDonald, Roman Catholic chaplain of Kingston penitentiary. One was dated May 3, 1912, another July 16,
1912,	and the third was issued in January,
1913.	These money orders, which were for small amounts, were sent by Mrs. McNeill, the mother of convict McNeill, who, I believe-although I am not sure of this- was one of the notorious Stoney mountain gang. This matter must have been brought to the attention of the minister. My first knowledge of the affair came from Inspector Hughes, who showed me the money orders in the inspector's office. It was there that I got the information and copied the dates and the amounts. I suppose that if the inspector of the penitentiary would give me the information, the Minister of Justice and the other inspector could not be unaware of the facts. Whether they were or not, the point I want to make is this: it would appear, and it does appear to some, that in the two cases that I have cited there was discrimination. As it happens, the'official who was dismissed at Stoney Mountain was a Protestant; the one who was not dismissed was a Roman Catholic. As it happens, the two officials who were dismissed, and properly so, at Kingston, were Protestants; the one who was not interfered with was a Roman Catholic.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman give me the names of the gentlemen to whom he is referring?

I cannot do so offhand. I think the minister can take my statement



for it that two guards were dismissed on that occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not questioning
that. The hon. gentleman is asking me to make a distinction between cases, and it is somewhat difficult for me to point out the distinction, if there he one, when I cannot lay my hand on the particular cases.

I can assure the hon.
minister that the two guards at Kingston were dismissed because they admitted that they had got money from outside persons; they had taken a commission on that money and conveyed the rest to the prisoners. 1 am not now saying for one moment that that is what Rev. Mr. McDonald did. I am not saying that he took a commission on the small amounts that were sent to him. But that does not make any difference; the regulations state that no official of the institution shall carry in letters, or carry out letters, or carry any money or any other article to a prisoner confined in the institution.
Does the hon. gentleman know what the money was used for?

No, I do not know what it was used for; I do not know whether it was used at all. I am not concerned about that. I am bringing this to the attention of the minister; it 'appears, without any explanation at all, as if there was discrimination. I am not saying that there was discrimination. On the contrary, I hope the minister will be able to give an explanation with regard to this matter that will demonstrate to the public that there was no discrimination whatever, and that there was good and sufficient reason for not dealing with Father McDonald, who apparently was the medium by which moneys were conveyed from the outside to the inside. We have in this Dominion people of different races and creeds, and it is up to the head of the Department of Justice, more than the head of any other department, to demonstrate to all races, classes and creeds in this country that there is no discrimination in these matters. It is incumbent upon him	to remove	any	suspicion	ofthat	kind, and	that	is why	I
refer to these matters. It would appear on the surface, and it has appeared to many, that there was discrimination. It appears to me as it has appeared to many down at Kingston, that some officials in the institution there can do things that others cannot do, and that some are punished for things in respect of which others are allowed

to go scot free. It became clear a very few years after the investigation of 1897, when the Liberal party came into power, that every guard, every keeper, every man who gave evidence on that occasion and whose testimony in any way affected or seemed to affect the higher officers, had to walk the plank. In time they got them; it took longer in some cases than it did in others. Since this last investigation came on it has been apparent that a certain clique and class in that institution are deliberately hounding the lives out of some men there, making unjustifiable charges against them in the determination of driving them out of the institution. That sort of thing will continue until it is made apparent that all men are going to be used alike in that institution, whether they are guards or whether they are prisoners. I say that they have not been used alike in the past. So far as the convicts are concerned, there has been discrimination. Men like Travers have got privileges which are not accorded to other convicts in that institution; certain guards have been accorded privileges which were not accorded to others.
I have no apology to make for my connection with the investigation into the affairs of the penitentiary at Kingston. I knew that, previous to 1911, things could not be right in that institution as it was then being conducted. I knew it was impossible for things to be right so long as ex-convicts were appointed as officials of the penitentiary, and that was the practice previous to 1911. Because of certain things which were brought to my attention which I thought should, be investigated, I made certain charges. I believe that, imperfect as that investigation was, it has resulted in good. I believe that the institution is better to-day than it Wias before the investigation, and that the removal, of insane convicts was a move in the Tight direction. I want to express my opinion that if something could be done along the lines of segregation, making special provision for young men, for the boys of 16, 18 and 20 years of age so as to keep them separate from the old and hardened criminals, that would be a great step in the direction of reform. But so long as proper employment is not found for the prisoners, so long as 60 or 70 men are allowed to work, day after day, and week after week, and year after year, at nothing more than breaking stones, the institution must be far from perfect, and the people of this country will be far from doing their duty by

the 2,000 men who are incarcerated within the walls of our various penal institutions. These men should be put at employment in which they would have some exercise for their minds as well as for their bodies; and until that is done the management of our institutions is not, in my judgment, all that it should he.
I wish again to enter my protest against this annuity being paid to Dr. Phelan, for the reasons I have already stated. I do not think that his course as an official in the institution warrants any such generous treatment as he is now receiving. I should also like an explanation from the minister of the particular cases to which I have referred, for the reasons I have stated. I have no doubt that he will be able to give such explanation to the committee.
Mr. McKENZIE .[DOT] Do I understand that
convicts are not permitted to have any money in their possession?
I think the rules are very strict against their having any money. Any money or valuables which they may have when they enter the institution are taken from them and kept safely until their release.

If it is at all permissible for a convict to have money, to receive a few dollars from relations or friends without the penitentiary, I should regard it as a very small offence on the part of the chaplain or any other official to take a money order received by a convict and get it cashed for him. If it were in circumstances of that kind that Rev. Father McDonald cashed the money order, even if he made a mistake, if it were his first offence, I should consider it a rather harsh rule that would cause his dismissal from office, if there were no other charges against him.

If that were the case I certainly would not see any ground for complaint; but that is not my understanding. I understand that the rules are very strict against officials conveying money or any papers to or from any convicts within the walls.	[DOT]
Do I understand that the Mr. Stewart referred to was a lawyer employed to assist the commission in the investigation? '
I presume that would be the position.

The hon. member for Frontenao has tried to make out a strong case against the minister for having recommended the superannuation of Dr. Phelan. I do not know Dr. Phelan, and I do not know if the hon. member's statement of the facts is absolutely correct. I shall not pass judgment on that because I do not know him, and do not know whether the allegations against him were all true. But I would remind the hon. member for Frontenac that the Minister of Justice is not the only sinner in superannuating officers or employees of this Government. The hon. member seems to think there was discrimination in the case of certain officers at Kingston. I would draw his attention to another case which occurred a few years ago. We had a law clerk of the House of Commons who was drawing a -salary of $3,350 a year at the time of his superannuation, in 1913. He was then only 48 years of age and had served only 17 years, yet 10 years were added to his time of service. The hon. member for Frontenac blames the Minister of Justice for adding 10 years service to the time of Dr. Phelan. Wh-at was the reason alleged for the superannuation of Mr. O'Brien? Abolition of office. But the office was- not abolished in reality; the name was changed from law clerk of the House of Commons to parliamentary counsel, but the office still exists and is well filled to-day by Mr. Gisborne, at a higher salary than Mr. O'Brien was getting, and the superannuation paid to Mr. O'Brien is larger than that paid to Dr. Phelan, being $1,741.50.
Mr. O'Brien is practising his profession to-day in the city of Toronto, and the country will have to pay him, perhaps for twenty-five or thirty years, the annual sum of $1,741.50. We know that there was an investigation held with regard to the conduct of that officer. Mr. O'Brien seemed to have what I might call the persecution mania. He thought he was persecuted by his assistant, who is, perhaps, the most inoffensive person employed by the Government. We were told that Mr. O'Brien carried a revolver to protect himself against his assistant. An investigation was held by the Speaker of this House, not the present Speaker, but his predecessor, and when he saw that he would have to report unfavourably against Mr. O'Brien, he refused to go further, and asked to be excused, My hon. friend from Frontenac said that there was discrimination in favour

*of Dr. Phelan because he was a Roman Catholic.
I never said anything of the kind.
I understood that he said there had been discrimination in favour of officers of the Kingston penitentiary who were Roman Catholics, as against those who were Protestants:

I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I did not say that. What I did say, and I thought I made it very clear, because I repeated it two or three times, was that I did not make a charge of discrimination, but I asked an explanation from the minister of what might appear to be discrimination. I further stated that I hoped that the minister would have an explanation which would show tnat no person was justified in having suspicion of discrimination. So far as Dr. Phelan is concerned, I did not mention his religion from first to last. In regard to Dr. Phelan's superannuation, it is not a question of whether a man who had performed his duties properly is entitled to superannuation. I am not arguing that; I am taking the ground that, in my judgment, Dr. Phelan was not a competent officer and had not performed his duties properly, and that, therefore, he was not entitled to superannuation, no matter how long he had served, whether 18 or 100 years. I do not say that superannuation is wrong if an official has proved a good official; my whole argument is that Phelan was not worthy of consideration, and should have been put out long before he was' because he was inefficient.

Perhaps I may have misunderstood my hon. friend, but I certainly understood him to say that there were some officers in the Stoney Mountain penitentiary who were punished, or dismissed, because they were Protestants.
One.

And that there were some officers in the Kingston Penitentiary who were not punished or dimissed because they were Roman Catholics. To return to what I was saying regarding the law clerk of the House of Commons',	the
Speaker asked to be excused from investigating the matter further, and the Government employed a lawyer in this city to continue the investigation. A report was made, but we have not been able to get it.
CMr. Proulx. ]
A motion was made by the hon. member for Laval (Mr. C.1 A. Wilson) for the production of that j'eport, and I remember that the right hon. the Prime Minister asked the hon. member for Laval to go to his private office and consult him about it. I do not know what transpired between them, but the report has never been presented to this House.
