speechtext: I have not interrupted the hon. member because I hoped that he was referring to that case by way of comparison. I hope he will not continue the discussion of the subject at any length.

I desire to refer to it
only by way of comparison, and I will be as short as possible. The gentleman referred to was transferred for a few months to the Department of Justice at a higher salary, I think $5,000 a year, to fill a position which had been created shortly before. I do not know what the reason was, but he did not stay there. Perhaps the Minister of Justice did not like to keep him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He did not like to stay; he retired.

He was retired, and the country has to pay $1,741.50 per year. It has been rumoured that very strong pressure was brought to bear on the Government by members of the society to which the gentleman belonged to induce it to grant him superannuation.
The hon. member for Frontenac blamed Inspector Hughes for a lot of the trouble which occurred at Kingston Penitentiary. Perhaps he is sorry to-day that he was responsible in a large degree for the appointment of Inspector Hughes. I remember that at one time Inspector Hughes was very anxious to be appointed warden of Kingston, and the hon. member for Frontenac got a petition signed by his Conservative confreres in the House asking the Minister of Justice to appoint Mr'. Hughes as warden. .	*
I did not get any petition signed.
Did the hon. member not sign a petition?
I did not sign a petition.

Did my hon. friend not
recommend Mr. Hughes for the position of warden?
I did.

When Mr. Hughes was not appointed warden he got the inspectorship. I can understand the hon. member for Fronteniac thinking that Inspector Hughes was not very grateful for the support of my hon. friend in getting the position of inspector because he went back on him, and would not help him to prosecute the investigation that my friend started at the penitentiary. He said that when Inspector Hughes got an increase of salary, his mind changed. I do not know to what extent his mind will change now that he is getting double salary, as the Minister of Justice admitted this afternoon. Besides getting his salary as inspector, he-is being paid a salary as lieutenant-colonel of the militia. I think my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) was right in stating that even if the chaplain had exchanged money orders for a few convicts, it should not have been made a crime against him. The hon. member for Fron-tenac said that things were going very badly at Kingston Penitentiary before 1911, but according to his own story, they seem to have been worse since that year. He stated that before 1911 some ex-convicts acted as guards, and he seemed to think that that was an awful thing. In these days, we are glad to keep ex-convicts out of this House. If all he said is true, I do not think the conditions have improved very much since 1911; indeed, I am rather inclined to think they are worse than they were in 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I desire to answer as briefly and as clearly as may be possible quite a few of the observations which the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has found it his duty to make in regard to certain matters in connection with Kingston penitentiary. The first matter to which he adverts is the manner in which the determination of the superannuation allowed to Dr. Phelan, upon the abolition of the office that he held, was made. He points out that whereas the amount paid to Dr. Phelan as superintendent was $1,512, he is replaced to-day by two gentlemen whose united remunerations amount to $1,360. So far as the statement of fact is concerned, he is correct., but I would like to point out that in the first place these ' two gentlemen are performing duties merely as surgeon or physician to the penitentiary, for which the salary formerly paid to Dr. Phelan was $1,700 a year, and that the annuity which he was given 'bears not only upon that salary, but upon the salary of $1,000 a year which he had as superintendent of the insane asylum, an office which neither of these gentlemen occupy. Furthermore, I think that it is fair to say that perhaps the reason the remuneration paid to these gentlemen is very moderate this year-and it certainly is very moderate-is to be found in the fact that the system which we have adopted of retaining two physicians-a visiting and a consulting physician-is a new sys-

tern, and inasmuch as neither of these two gentlemen give their entire service, the whole amount that could be allowed under the statute is $1,360 between the two. We have but one salary for a-surgeon. Should this new plan which is being tested prove a success-and I think the hon. gentleman agrees with me in hoping that it will be- it is not impossible that it might be considered a larger remuneration ought to be paid; but that is a matter for future consideration, the two gentlemen being satisfied for the time being to assume the duties under the conditions mentioned. But I understand that substantially the criticism rests upon the fact that the hon. member for Frontenac does not think that the conduct of Dr. Phelan, while he held his office, jusified his being allowed the annuity which he was allowed. I understand, more particularly from an answer made by the hon. gentleman to some observation made by the hon. member for Prescott, that that is the gravamen of his complaint. The hon. gentleman did point out, however, that out of 45 employees who had been retired this year, the case of Dr. Phelan was the only one where this additional ten years was allowed. I presume that he is correct in that statement of fact, though I have not had occasion to look into it myself. But I should like to point out that there is absolutely nothing to show that any of the other 44 came within either the one or the other of the two sections of the statute under which Dr. Phelan came, arid under which this additional ten years is permissible; so that unless some of those gentlemen came within those conditions, there is no conclusion whatever to be drawn from the fact that they were not granted the ten years. I am not prepared to affirm that none of them did; but I have no knowledge that any of them did, and I do not understand that the hon. gentleman contends himself that they did, or is in a position to say that they did. But I can say this without any fear, though there may have been some, there certainly were not 44. The House will have noticed the conditions under which this may be done, and those conditions make the cases where it may be done very exceptional indeed. So that necessarily the men who are granted the additional ten years, as compared with the bulk of the men who retire or are superannuated, are a very small number. But, as I have said, the gravamen of the complaint is that by reason of the conduct of Dr. Phelan he should not have obtained the advantage 
which, under the statute, the conditions in which he found himself entitled him to, or, at all events,- put him in a position to receive. I do not desire to take up longer time than is absolutely necessary in any discussion of the conduct of Dr. Phelan. I desire, however, to meet as fully as I can, what has been said upon the subject.
It is first said that Dr. Phelan was unworthy of receiving this, because of two findings with regard to particular charges made by the commission which investigated the affairs of Kingston penitentiary. The first of these, as the hon. member for Frontenac stated it, is that Dr. Phelan was found guilty of having used violent and filthy language, so violent and filthy "that it would not be allowed to print it." Now, each one can supply his own qualifications of the language that a man used. The commission in its report does not use quite as strong a language in describing the words attributed to Dr. Phelan a-s the hon. member for Frontenac used. Their finding is:
The charge of using violent and indecent language to a guard In the presence of others is established; hut it is claimed that it was used in jest. The finding leaves this uncertain.
So that the finding of the commission was that, whatever the language may have been, it was uncertain whether it was used in earnest or jest. They go on to say;
In any case the surgeon entirely forgot the dignity of his position and the discipline of the prison in making use of the language he did, and the incident discloses an unhealthy state of things.	.
In effect, therefore, it was found that upon this particular occasion the surgeon forgot the dignity of his position and the discipline of the prison in making use of the language. That, no doubt, is not commendable. The question, however, is not whether that was absolutely commendable or not, but whether that, with the other things mentioned, was a sufficient reason why Dr. Phelan in effect should, if his office had not been abolished, have been dismissed; because unless he should have been, he would have been entitled to go on, and, if he had lived, in course of time would have got the addition that is now in question. While I appreciate the delicacy which makes the hon. member for Frontenac refrain from repeating the language attributed to Dr. Phelan, I do think that justice requires of us that we should-how should I express it? harden our ears, and I am going to ask the House to stand the horror of listening to these horrible words.

I understand them to have been described as being of the most indecent kind, and the impression made upon my mind by the remarks of the hon. member for Fron-tenac was that he considered them-and in fact represented them-as being something of extreme indecency.
In fact, if my note is correct, he indicated that it was such violent and filthy language that it could not be .allowed to he printed. Now, as I said, I am going to ask the House to stand listening to a repetition of these words, for if Dr. Phelan is to be judged for his use of these words, and my *conduct in judging of them is to .be approved or disapproved, it 'is only fair that the House should know what they were. So, if the House will get itself together so as to be able to stand the awful shook, I will read the words:
Dr. Phalen was standing in front of the warden's offlse in the passage lead ng into the prison. As soon as he saw me-
That is, the witness, George AikenS.
-he siid-
Now, Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, I hope you will be able to stand it:
-Hullo! you damned big tub of guts, your holidays are over.
I suppose we had better wait until we get our breath again. The other thing that he said-I do not know whether you will find it worse or not-is thus reported:
You are the damnedest crank and the God damnedest disturber X ever seen.
You will notice that the grammar is open to criticism. I do not say that this is elegant language. But I ask in all fairness and common sense, of a gathering of men who have sometimes listened to language that is on occasion used even by people occupying more lofty positions than that of surgeon of a penitentiary and superintendent of .an insane ward in a penitentiary, whether their ears have not sometimes been smitten with words even more indecent than that, even-if I might say so-even proceeding from the lips of a member of Parliament.
Never.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I ask, in all seriousness, if one of us had a doctor in attendance upon him and found him a competent doctor, and his treatment all that it ought to be, and if we were informed that the doctor had used just that language to somebody outside, should we think that we ought
to dismiss that doctor? And now, you are further to remember that the answer was, not that the language had not been used, but that it was used in jest; and the commission report that that remains uncertain, but they do find that the doctor lacked in dignity on that occasion. I think this is a case in which he among us who is without sin had better be allowed to cast the first stone; or, I think I might say, has cast the first stone. The rest of us, who may not be without sin, I am sure will refrain from casting stones.

If I may be permitted -of course, it is a matter of indifference to me whether the hon. minister regards the language as nice or otherwise-as to the question of it being used in jest, Dr. Phelan felt so seriously about it, at all events, that he endeavoured to get one of the men who heard him use the language to enter the witness box and perjure himself with regard to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will come to that in a moment-I like to take these things one thing at a* time. The hon. gentleman says iit is immaterial to him whether I think this language nice or not. Well, I do not think it nice. But I do not think that the use of it would justify me in saying that the man who used it was unworthy of holding the position that he held-even making the very worst of it. I do not know what the judgment of this House may be on that matter, but I leave it to their judgment. It is said that the language was so bad that the doctor tried to induce somebody to commit perjury about it. It is true there is one witness who said the doctor talked the matter over with him, and to whom he said, as he said to the commission, that he had used the language, but had used it in jest, ahd he said to this witness: You might say you did not hear it. That is not a suggestion that it was desirable to make, either. But exactly what meaning is to be attached, to these words, I think, is a matter of question. To say that they meant that he asked the man to commit perjury is, I think, perhaps, straining things. I do not think he ought to have said that. But it stands on the mere statement of one witness-no doubt telling the truth as he recollects it, but putting, no doubt, his own interpretation on what was said to him. Dr. Phelan may have been over-nervous and may have been anxious that thife gentleman should coincide with his view that he had used these words in

jest, and even may have thought it possible that the man ought to say that he had not heard it. I take it for what it is worth, but he did say that the man might say he had not heard it. It is to be noted that the commissioners express no condemnation and that they rest no decision upon it, one way or the other. I take it for what it is worth, and I cannot see that it is a reason why that to which Dr. Phelan was entitled by eighteen years of service should 'be withdrawn from him.
There is a second accusation-or, perhaps, I should say a third, because this point of the witness not having heard the ' words is made part of the case-and that is, that Dr. Phelan' had been a petty grafter, in that he had charged four different guards-not guards, it is well to point out, but applicants for appointment to the position of guard-a dollar apiece for examining them. It is to be noted that the commission does not find that that action on his part was the getting of money for the performance of anything that it was his duty to perform for the salary he received, for it was no part of his duty as surgeon of the penitentiary to attend people who were not, as yet, employees. He is condemned by the commission, not because it was his duty to make these examinations for nothing, but because, under the terms of his agreement, he was not allowed to carry on general practice, and, therefore, he should not have collected money for services rendered to anybody outside the penitentiary. I am quite prepared, to accept the view of the commission with regard to that, and I take it as established that Dr. Phelan committed himself to that extent.
So far as charges brought against him directly and categorically are concerned, these are the things found to rest against him-that he used the language I have repeated, though it is uncertain whether he used it in jest or not, that it was not dignified language, and that he had received $4, being a foliar apiece from four applicants, which was a violation of his obligation not to do outside practice. The hon. gentleman has pointed out the serious responsibilities that belong to my position as Minister of Justice. I am not blind to those serious responsibilities. I have the responsibility, not specially, perhaps, because I am Minister of Justice, but as a Minister of the Crown, of trying to deal justly with everybody who comes under my authority. I am prepared to say

that it would be impossible for me to reconcile to my sense of justice the dismissal of a gentleman occupying the position that Dr. Phelan did upon the grounds of the three things that have been stated here. I am in the judgment of tnis committee as to whether or not that is a proper conclusion. I do not say that the language was desirable language to use, and I am prepared to say that I think Dr. Phelan should not have collected those $4; but I could not reconcile it to my sense of justice to say that for those two things I would have been right in depriving him of that which the law entitled him to upon the abolition of his office and after his eighteen years of service, when he had reached the age of 61 years.
Was he not in a position to continue his services to the penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He was in a position
to do it, if his office had not been abolished.
But the minister has appointed two others in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not to the office that
he held. He was me physician attached to the penitentiary, bound to give his exclusive service to that institution, and he was the superintendent of the insane ward. For those services he received a salary of $2,700 a year. That position has now ceased to exist; there is no insane ward, and, therefore, there can be no superintendent. Further, we have changed our system of employment of physicians. We retain no one as exclusively the surgeon to the penitentiary; we employ outside medical men to give attendance at the penitentiary, they remaining free to carry on their practice. That was not the position to which Dr. Phelan had been appointed and which he had accepted, and we were not in a position to compel him to accept that new position under those different conditions. The positions which he had occupied were abolished, and under the statute he was absolutely entitled to his superannuation. The only matter concerning which there was question was the addition of the ten years. His office had been abolished, but in addition to that there was the fact that he had come into the service when he was more than 30 years old, and had come in because of special professional qualifications. The statute authorizes the Governor in Council in either of those cases to make the addition of ten years; we were face to face with a case where "both of

those conditions existed. The gravamen of the objection of the hon. member for Fron-tenac is not that it was improper to do this, but that it was done in an improper ease by reasons of the shortcomings of Dr. Phelan during his holding of office.
There is another matter that is referred to by the hon. gentleman, which, if Dr. Phelan be the person properly to bear the responsibility, and if the conditions were as grave as the hon. member for Frontenae describes them, is a much more serious matter for consideration than the particular matters which I have referred to. The particular matters which I have referred to form part of special charges brought against Dr. Phelan by the hon. member for Froo-tenac. The matter that I am now going to refer to is one that did not come under the head of any of these charges; it is one which the commission, in the performance of their general duty of looking into the state and management of the penitentiary, had their attention brought to and with regard to which they made certain observations. That matter covers the management of the insane ward and the conditions under which it was carried on, and the general hospital conditions that prevailed in the institution. If there never had been any commission appointed and an investigation made, I should have adopted the course which I have since adopted with regard to the insane ward. I myself formed the opinion, not very long after I had come to occupy the position that I now occupy, and after one or two visits to the penitentiary and some consideration of the subject, that an insane ward, an adjunct of a penitentiary, carried on under penitentiary management, was no suitable place for insane people, even though they were convicts. I say that I had formed that opinion, but as I had thought it desirable 'to have an inquiry into the general conditions of the penitentiary, I did think it was not- unwise to let that matter, as well as others, be passed upon by the commissioners, that I might have the benefit of their advice. Upon the subject of the existence of the insane ward their opinion coincided with mine, and their report has since been acted on by the transference ol the insane convicts to the insane asylums of the different provinces. That the system was wrong there is not any doubt in my judgment. The system is condemned by the report of the commissioners. It is condemned by Dr. Phelan in his own evidence, and fault is found with him because
his reports year by year apparently showed everything to be right in connection with the administration of the insane ward. It is just to Dr. Phelan to say that he did not create the system. He found the system in existence when he went there, and it continued in existence until its recent abolition. So far, therefore, as the system itself was concerned, Dr. Phelan was not responsible for it.
It is said that the amount of attention given to the insane patients was not sufficient. But Dr. Phelan was not given the insane ward with the proper attendance for an insane ward; he was there in. the joint capacity of superintendent of the insane ward and surgeon of the penitentiary, -and I do not find it suggested that he was lacking in any duty that under that system his superior officers called on him to perform.
He might have been a more forceful man and might have protested against the system; but we must remember that we are dealing with an employee and that the responsibility for the system rested with his employers.
With regard to the hospital conditions, they, too, are criticised and condemned by the commission. I do not now pretend to go into the whole question of the evidence upon which that condemnation rests. My own disposition in such a case is that, wherever there is anything that in the judgment of reasonable men may be reasonably susceptible of improvement, an effort should be made to effect such improvement. The question that arises here is, who had the responsibility for the conditions that existed? The commission says that the responsibility should be shared between the surgeon and the inspectors. But this fact remains, that the conditions, whatever they may have been, which they condemned, existed, and, as appears by the report itself, to the full knowledge of the superior officers of Dr. Phalen; and these officers expressed no dissatisfaction with those conditions. It is true that it was suggested that Dr. Phelan might have reported upon those conditions; but the commissioners themselves say that, while he might have done that, it does appear that those conditions were known to his superiors. I am not dealing with the question of whether something better might not have been done by Dr. Phelan, but with the question of how the matter should be dealt with, and the question of whether or not he was responsible for the conditions

that existed, and so should have laid upon his shoulders the entire burden of responsibility and the punishment to be allotted, if punishment were called for. I have given to this matter the most careful consideration of which I am capable. I have read the evidence as it bears upon Dr. Phelan, and I have read the report of the commissioners; I have listened with attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Frontenae this afternoon, as I have done on previous occasions.
What is the minister's own opinion with regard to the conditions in the hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think there was room for great improvement in the conditions at the hospital, but those conditions were what one might call the physical conditions.
I did not refer to it in that connection, but has the minister any doubt that there was tubbing of insane prisoners?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Recently?
I did not say recently.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How far back does the testimony with reference to tubbing go?
The minister knows that the investigation was limited to a period of five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I limited it to five
years, but I made an exception for any matter anterior , to the five years which the commissioners might consider had any bearing on the actual condition of affairs. Under that proviso very many matters that dated back more than five years were gone into. But I ask this House whaA interest have we in investigating to-day whether five years ago or four years ago, under the control of men who are not now in the penitentiary, there was or was not tubbing? The important thing is that there is none going on to-day, and, unless it has a bearing on the question of Dr. Phelan's treatment- and it is conceded that it has not

I produce that report
to show that the report of the inspectors was false.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then, I have got it in the wrong order. The hon. gentleman says that Mr. Carlyle said that if some one would show him the man that some one hon-

oured, he would be able to appreciate the value of the man who did so. I do not know that I feel called upon to make exhibitions of the people I have honoured. In many ways I would be pleased to honour the hon. member for Frontenac; so that the exact application of Mr. Carlyle's observation does not strike me. It was not a question of honouring Dr. Phelan or of not honouring him; it was a question of doing our duty, as justice required us to do, in dealing with this officer whose connection with the Government had ceased. We were not of opinion that there had been established against him such fault as would justify us of depriving him of that which might be granted to him under the law. I gave my best thought to that question; what I thought then I think now, and I am willing to take the judgment of this House, and of the public, for what I did.
A statement was made by the hon. gentleman about supper having been given to the prisoners at a very early hour on Sundays, almost immediately after their lunch. There is some difference of opinion as to whether or not that was done on more than one occasion. I am not going to enter into any discussion of the matter, but let us assume that it was done; it certainly is not done now. I do not propose to enter into the discussion, which the hon. member entered upon, as to the truthfulness of the report of Inspectors, Stewart and Hughes. Their report is to the minister conveying to him their views. It is, in the first place, their statement of facts as they see the facts in connection with what goes on in the penitentiary.	The particular report
referred to did give their views upon the effect of evidence that was produced before the commission.	The commission had
made a report which, in some respects, reflected upon the inspectors. The inspectors, when they came to make their report to the minister, thought themselves entitled to make their answers. I do not understand, and I have no doubt the hon. member for Frontenac does not understand, that the report is the work of the minister. It is a report to the minister, and the minister would not be justified in saying to these officers that they must report to him otherwise than in accordance with their own judgment and their own views. I am not therefore going to go over again this discussion as to whether or not they are right in so far as they differ from the commission, or whether the commission is

right. Nor am I going to discuss the question of whether they are right or whether the hon. member for Frontenac is right in so far as he differs with them as regards their statement of the facts with reference to what has occurred in the past. I do not know that there would be any purpose served by my taking sides in that discussion. I may say that my great concern is to discover what can be done to-day to make things better. Whether somebody was wrong a year ago, or two years ago, or three years ago, seems to me a matter that, from the point of view of the administration of the penitentiary, and as bearing upon the future conduct of the penitentiary, is immaterial.
As far as Go!. Hughes is concerned, I do not know but that perhaps it might have been thought that there would be a truce on the subject. Col. Hughes to-night is in the trenches somewhere in France. Col. Hughee is not here to answer attacks made upon him, as he is facing the shell fire of the enemy and the attacks of German snipers. I thought that perhaps under the circumstances matters involving accusations against Col. Hughes might have been allowed to stand until his return. The hon. member for Frontenac was quite within his rights in determining whether it v^as necessary or useful that he should refer to these matters. But I point out that Col. Hughes's absence puts me in a position where I have no means of putting before the House what may be the reply, if there be a reply, of Col. Hughes to what has been said in regard to him.
I said nothing whatever about Col. Hughes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Inspector Hughes.
Inspector Hughes is the man I was referring to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is Col. Hughes.
He is W. S. Hughes. I was referring to W. S. Hughes, inspector of penitentiaries. I have nothing to say about Col. Hughes at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The gentleman who is W. S. Hughes, inspector of penitentiaries, happens to be Col. Hughes.
I have nothing to do with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, he has only one physical personality, and as colonel, being in the trenches this evening, it is not pos-

sible far him, as inspector, to be here. I refer to it merely as explaining why, were it proper I should do so, it is impossible for me to convey to the House any thing he might desire said by way of reply. I do not, however, think it is material to inquire what are the exact merits of this difference of opinion, or this difference of statement in regard, to facts as between Inspector Hughes and the hon. member for Frontenac. I do not propose, therefore, to go into a discussion of the criticism which the hon. gentleman has made of the report of the inspectors.
There are some specific things that he has said, though, that I would like to meet. It has been said that there was gross discrimination as between convicts. This has been specified to the extent of a statement with regard to Travers, a convict detained in the penitentiary, that while he was there he had been furnished with money, that 'he had been treated differently from other prisoners, that he had cigars and a pipe, and that when he was, under order of the court, taken to Toronto to give testimony, he was allowed to order liquor. This is the first time I have heard the statement that any such thing had happened. My officers report to me that the hon. gentleman is misinformed; but I want to say here that if there is evidence to establish that I will be glad to have it at my disposal in order that I may deal with those who may be responsible. In the meantime, it is fair to my officers to say that their report is that the hon. member has been misinformed. Then, also, it should be pointed out that if anything of the kind had happened, in so far as the statement of what occurred in Toronto is concerned, while Travers remained in Toronto at the disposition of the court, he was then, as I understand it, under control of the prison authorities there.
The hon. gentleman made some criticism in connection with the investigation of the commissioner?, more particularly in reference to a prisoner named Rose. We had some considerable discussion at the last session of Parliament with regard to the action of thepe commissioners, during which my hon. friend expressed his opinion in regard to them. I then said what I conceived to be proper in that connection, and I do not deem it necessary to add anything to my statement to-night.
But there were some things in particular to which the hon. member called my attention, because he said he wanted to give me
an opportunity to make an explanation. As I understood him, there were two matters which he states occurred at Kingston, and two matters which he states occurred at Stoney Mountain penitentiary. As to the statement of facts, I understand his suggestion is that some people might conclude that there was some disposition on my part to discriminate as between employees, and that the facts would indicate that that discrimination turned upon their respective religious beliefs. If I might say one personal thing, it would be that after having lived to be 60 years of age in a community of Catholics and Protestants, it is a little difficult for me to keep a serious face when I find it seriously suggested that it makes a difference to me whether the man with whom I am dealing is a Catholic or a Protestant. That is where it strikes me personally. But I recognize that, inasmuch it has been suggested that under my rule, some people may believe that something of the kind may take place, and I therefore realize that it is important that the suggestion should be met. I find no fault with the hon. gentleman for asking me for an explanation. In regard to the Kingston penitentiary, he says that there were two guards who happened to be Protestants, and who, having admitted that, in violation of the rule, in fact, I think, of the statute,	they had brought money
in to	convicts,	were discharged.
That is true. What he contrasts with that is a case with regard to the Roman Catholic chaplain in the Kingston Penitentiary. I understood him to say that it transpired towards the end of the investigation that was had by the Royal Commission, that there was evidence that the reverend gentleman had committed the same offence, that is, that he had brought money in to convicts. I want to be correct.
I did not say that, because I did not know that to be a fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not stating it as a fact.

I appreciate that the
minister wants to be correct. I said that the evidence provided by his inspector showed that three money orders had been cashed by the Reverend Mr. McDonald. I called his attention to the fact that since the money came from the mother of one of the convicts, the presumption was that it was for the convict. I consider that the minister should have investigated and

found out the facts. Perhaps the money was for the priest himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to point
out just what we did .after that was called to my attention. It was ascertained in connection with the inquiry that quite a number of letters, some of them registered, I think, and some of them containing money orders, had come to different persons, connected with the penitentiary from persons related to different convicts, and among those to whom such letters had come was the Reverend Father McDonald. There were quite a number of these letters, certainly some twenty or twenty-five.
What was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The names were on a list which was handed me by the inspectors, I believe. There were quite a number of them; their religions, of course, I do not know. Whether I first saw the names on a list, or a list was made from other documents or sources of information, I do not know. At all events, a list was finally shown me. After I had heard the statement about Mr. McDonald-and the first time I heard it was when the hon. gentleman made it in the House-I made inquiry, and was told that there were a number of such cases, with regard to which the suggestion was that some individual should be appointed to look into them, as it was not thought necessary to carry on the entire commission to look into these details. What I did in this regard was to have the different people written to who had appeared to have received registered letters, asking for an explanation of the letters they had received. I received explanations from all of them, and those explanations on their faces looked to be satisfactory. One man said that the money he received was for the purposes of making payments to a building society. Different explanations were given, and the answers seemed reasonable. The Rev. Father McDonald's explanation was that he had received money orders from the mother of a convict. Perhaps there was a presumption that that money went or may have gone to the convict. Rev. Father McDonald took the position that he was not at liberty to divulge the purpose for which the money had come to him, and though perhaps one might have been justified in not pushing inquiries further, I did push them further, and asked for a further explanation. The sender of that money-the mother of this convict-sent the following document:

This is to certify that I have never, at any time, sent any money to Rev. Father McDonald, of Portsmouth, for the purpose of having the same paid to my son, now confined in Kingston penitentiary. I have had several communications with the sai'd Rev. Father McDonald, relating to matters of a private and confidential character, and being such were intended for R:v. Father McDonald alone, and of which he has no right to make disclosures to anybody else, and cannot properly do so without committing a breach of confidence.
I leave it in all fairness whether I should try to force the mother of this unfortunate boy to reveal those things which she says were of a confidential nature between her and her clergyman. I think the hon. member will recognize himself that until I have some evidence other than I have, I should not be justified in setting on foot an investigation that could only be satisfied by compelling that woman to reveal what were the purposes for which she gave this money to the priest who occupied the position which he did.
What about compelling the man who got the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This woman says he
could not reveal the purpose for which he got the money without a breach of confidence, and, very properly, he says he will not Teveal it. Here we have the woman's positive statement that the money was not to go to her son. I want to say. quite frankly that it is a matter of absolute indifference to me to what church or denomination a clergyman might belong, but in the face of a statement such as I have read, I do not believe that the finding out where the money went is of such importance as to justify me forcing the revealing of what this woman communicated to the priest, presumably her spiritual adviser, in absolute confidence. I am not going to say, in the face of that statement, that there is such grave suspicion of wrong doing on the part of the clergyman, that I am going to undertake to .force the revelation of a confidential communication between this woman and her clergyman.
There seems to be no doubt that the gentleman received the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no doubt.

If the money was not given to the convict, there is no fault; but, if it was given to the convict, the prison rules were violated, just as in the cases which caused the dismissal of the other two fellows; they were not quite wise

enough to say that they had conscientious scruples about revealing the matter. 'My point is that whether it is Rev. Father McDonald, or reverend this, that or the other, a Roman' Catholic priest or a Protestant clergyman, he is a man in an official capacity, and has no more right to violate the regulations than any other man.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He has no more right to violate the regulations than any other man. But before I proceed to investigate, I must have evidence that he did violate the regulations. More than that, he received money from the mother of this convict, and she tells us categorically and clearly that it was not for her son, but it was for purposes and in connection with matters absolutely confidential between her and the clergyman.

I did not understand
the minister to say that before. If the lady said the money was'not for her son, of course, that is a different matter. My whole point was that that money was conveyed to the prisoner, which constituted a violation of the regulation, and he had no more right to violate the regulation than anybody else.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no question
about that. Here is the lady's statement:
This is to certify that I have never, at any time, sent any money to Rev. Father McDonald, of Portsmouth, for the purpose of having the same paid to my son, now confined in. Kingston penitentiary. I have had several communications with the said Rev. Father McDonald, relating to matters of a private and' confidential character, and, being such, were intended for Rev. Father McDonald alone, and of which he has no right to make disclosures to anybody else, and cannot properly do so without committing a breach of confidence.
She begins by saying she never sent any money to be delivered to her son.

My contention is that if Father McDonald conveyed the money to the convict, he violated the regulations, and that no priest or clergyman who is an official should be treated any differently from any other official.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Some people think that in dealing with absolutely confidential matters, they should make no answer. You may have one confidential thing where it is quite possible for you to make an answer, yes, or no; but you may have another confidential thing in regard to which, if you begin answering questions, conclusions may be drawn. In the face of this declaration, I, for one-and I may say that my view was
concurred in by my officers-thought that we were not called upon to proceed further.
Now, there is another question, also, with regard to the Catholic chaplain of a penitentiary. It is said that at Stoney Mountain penitentiary a guard was dismissed for passing letters in to a convict; and that the Roman Catholic chaplain was charged with the same offence, and was not dismissed. In fact it is said-and it is perfectly true-that upon the warden telegraphing to the minister that he had suspended the chaplain, the minister telegraphed the warden asking him to suspend the suspension and to forward to him, the minister, by telegraph, the facts of the case; and the chaplain was not dismissed. These things are perfectly true. There was different action in these cases; but it was because the cases were of an absolutely different nature, different in their circumstances, different in their gravity, and different, above all, in the guilty knowledge of the man who was concerned.
The guard who was dismissed was named McArthur. Let me read the report of the inspector who investigated this case, and upon whose report the guard was dismissed:
I ascertained from Canadian Northern railway headquarters that Trofton-
He was a former convict who was corresponding with a convict named Tucker in the penitentiary.
-was still at St. Norbert, and went out and got his sworn testimony in which he swears he sent convict Fuller four or five letters and received seven or eight from him, all while the said Fuller was in the penitentiary. He swears he sent all the letters addressed to Mr. John McArthur, Stony Mountain, and got all Fuller's letters through McArthur. He also swears he sent to John McArthur fifteen dollars in cash, same being sent at different times.
So we have four or five letters and fifteen dollars in cash going to this convict. Furthermore, it appears that on toeing examined, McArthur at first denied the charge, but when this evidence of the man who had sent the letters was put before him, he admitted it and admitted also that he fully knew he wae doing wrong.
Now, what was the case of Father Jou-bert, chaplain? I do not know just how long after Father Joulbert's appointment, but very shortly after, the warden found that Father Joubert had taken a letter out for' a convict. The warden himself thought that the proper thing was to call Father Joubert's attention to the fact that this

was a violation of the rule, and he did so. Father Joubert 6aid that he had not given thought to it, and that it should not happen again. What led to the suspension, was that, after this conversation, the warden found that another letter had been sent out, and apparently was under the impression that this had been done after Father Joubert's promise that it should not happen again, and he suspended him at once. That fact was telegraphed to me. I asked to have the suspension suspended, and to have the grounds of the warden's action communicated to me. So far as that action of. mine is concerned, independent of the final decision, I want to say quite frankly that I do not think you can deal with a chaplain, as regards the warden's power of summary suspension, as you might deal with a police officer. And for; this very simple reason-that we conduct ohr penitentiaries upon the principle that a valuable aid in the carrying on of the work of the penitentiary is the bringing to 'bear upon the convict of such religious influences as he -may he responsive to. I am not here to discuss whether that is wise or not"; all I say is that it is the system.
Personally of course I think it is wise. But, whatever I may think about it, that is the -system. If that system is to work effectively, surely our officers mu4t bear in mind the importance of letting it appear clear to the convict whom we seek to influence that thp minister of religion, whatever may he his denomination, is a person to 'be dealt with respectfully. He -must not be allowed to violate rules with impunity, but he is to be dealt with respectfully. And I have taken the position, with regard to a chaplain, Catholic or Protestant, that if there is ground of complaint against him, it is a proper matter to refer to the minister, and we will tey to do justice; and that, as long as there is a telegraph in existence which enables the warden to communicate speedily with the minister, there is no need for him to suspend the chaplain instaniter. I think that is a necessary requirement for the maintenance of proper respect for a man in th-e chaplain's position, and it is one that can do no possible injury to the penitentiary system.
So much for my request for the suspension. As to the offence itself and its beinj; dealt with, it was discovered, after the warden had _ so promptly suspended,

that he was mistaken in the supposition that there had been any repetition of the offefi-ee after attention had been called to it and the promise made. What did happen was that he came across a letter which had been sent previous to his observations on the subject, so that there had been no repetition of the offence, as the warden 'Supposed there had been after he gave the warning. These letters were in -themselves perfectly harmless, carried as they were to the relatives of the prisoner. Here on the one hand we have this offence of a newly appointed chaplain who, when it was pointed out to him, immediately expressed his Tegret, showing that he did it with thoughtlessness. On the other hand, we have the offence of a man who was carrying a series of letters between a convict and an ex-convict, and receiving money for the ex-convict. This man at first denied the offence, and only admitted it when he was confronted with the sworn testimony of the man who had sent him the letters. Then, of course, he acknowledged that he knew that it was entirely wrong 'to do this. These are the two cases. This guard was a Protestant; there is no doubt about that. I know it because the hon. gentleman has told me, and I take his word, but at the time I had no knowledge as to his religion.
I doubt the necessity of these explanations, but I do not know whether people believe that we investigate the religion of these different officers before we deal with them when charges are made. For my part, I do not do so. I suppose that if I am open to the suspicion, my statement is not worth much; but if -any one suspects that, I want to say for myself that I make no investigation as to a man's -religion. There is n-o doubt that it is unavoidable when the matter of a chaplain has to be dealt with., but my knowing his religion in that case does not affect my method of action.	These are the two cases.
I	leave	it to	the judgment of
this committee whether any improper motive may be atributed to me in the action that was taken. The action that was taken with regard to the guard was taken upon the recommendation of Inspector Hughes- whose Protestantism is, I think, beyond doubt. As regards the suspension of the suspension, I followed the rule that I have always followed with regard to chaplains. It happens that attention is called to my action with regard to Catholic chaplains; I have no doubt it is because these are the only cases that have been brought to the

hon. gentleman's attention. In one or two instances I have had to deal with questions concerning Protestant chaplains; in these cases there was no ground to find fault with the reverend gentlemen, and I did not find it necessary to take any action. I dealt with them myself, because I thought that was the proper way to deal with complaints against the chaplains. It is not in the interests of good administration that the warden should summarily suspend a chaplain, and I can see no evil coming from the minister's dealing with questions concerning these gentlemen. I do see in it a guarantee for maintenance among the convict population of that respect for these gentlemen which is absolutely essential to their being useful in the work which they do. The very head and front of my offending goes to that extent and no further, and I have no apology to make for it. If the case of the guard McArthur had been on all fours with the case of Father Joubert, I should have dealt with it in the same way; but it was totally different, and I dealt with it as I thought justice and good discipline required. The hon. member for Frontenac, since he has had reason to believe that there was a motive-which, as a matter of fact, did not exist-behind the action in regard to these things, has acted quite rightly and properly in affording me this opportunity of explaining the circumstance. I have an abiding confidence that fair-minded people-and the great bulk of our population, no matter what their religion may be, are fair-minded people-will he satisfied with the explanation that I have given, and that they will continue, at all events those who have known me in the past, to believe that no question of a man's religion weighs in the balance when I am called upon to try to do justice as between two individuals, or with regard to any one individual with whom fault may be found.
The hon. gentleman concluded with some observations with regard to improvements that might be made in our. penitentiary system, and adverted to the continued existence of the stone-pile and the necessity of useful employment. I do not think there is any difference of opinion between himself and .myself on that subject. I have listened, not only this evening, but on other occasions, to the hon. gentleman speak at greater length upon the general question of improvements that might be made in our penitentiary system. I may say, speaking generally, that I have sympathized very largely vrith the views that he expressed.
135	'
I should be very glad if it were practically possible for me to provide useful occupation within our penitentiaries for the men who are employed there, and I do look forward to being able to bring into existence a' system under which that may be done. We had this matter threshed out in the session of 1914, and I was looking forward vefy hopefully then to modification of our legislation with regard to penitentiaries, and to being able to make some arrangement by which, in connection with the other departments here, our penitentiary men might be employed in supplying their wants. But there came the war, and the great bulk of our people outside the penitentiaries were almost entirely dependent upon being employed in connection with things that were being made for the Government. Strong as was my desire to improve the conditions in the penitentiaries, I did not feel that that was an opportune moment for us to introduce the labour of the penitentiary in competition for the supplying of things that the Government might require. I do hope-we all do hope-for better days in that regard, and when the time comes I can assure the hon. gentleman that he will not be more anxious than I am to bring about improvement in the direction that he mentioned. Perhaps I may venture to hope that at that time I may have the valuable assistance of his cooperation and his suggestions as to what would be the best lines upon which we could carry out a policy of that kind. In the meantime, we have been endeavouring in a small way to improve conditions as they exist in Kingston penitentiary, and we hope to be able to extend that effort. I have put in a very considerable period of time in	working upon
an improved system	of regulation.
What I can do without changing the legislation-because I feel that I cannot legislate on the subject now-I am anxious to do; but that work has been delayed. A whole plan and scheme of new regulations has been prepared, but I have desired and still desire personally to go over them with a view to seeing how best I can improve the existing conditions. This has necessarily delayed the work. There are, unfortunately, many other things that call for a man's personal attention. We are working there, as I have said, short of one of our good inspectors, which increases the work to be done by the others. While I cannot claim any great achievement, I do assure this House, in all sincerity, that the



work of .improvement in penitentiary conditions is one in which I am greatly interested. and that I am very desirous of bringing about some improvements that will be really effective. I hope that when that time comes I may have the advantage of the counsel and co-operation of my hon. friend the member for Frontenac, who has taken so much interest in the conditions in these institutions.

I am very glad to assure the minister that in so far as the management of penitentiaries is concerned, and the improvement of their conditions, if he does me the honour, at any time in the future, to consider an opinion from me in that matter worthy of his consideration, I shall be only too glad to do anything I can to aid in that good work. I said this afternoon that some improvements had been made at Kingston since this investigation was held. It was an improvement to remove the insane convicts from that institution. I am led to believe that since the investigation there has been no tubbing of convicts and that the hose has not been used. These are steps in the right direction. I hope the time will come when we shall be able to segregate the younger convicts, the boys who are serving their first sentences, and that in the very near future men who are now pounding out their lives and souls on the stone-pile will be given useful employment, and that the stone-pile will be done away with. This will be a great step in the right direction.
In regard to the case of Rev. Father Joubert, of Stoney Mountain, the minister said that McArthur's dismissal was recommended to him by Inspector Hughes. I think that the removal of McArthur was perfectly right. He had deliberately violated the regulations. I- may say that my informant in regard to these two cases was the man who recommended to the minister the removal of McArthur. Those eases are not the only ones to which I might have referred, and which did give colour to the suspicion that there was a difference in the treatment of guards and others in the penitentiaries; and that, added to the very positive and emphatic statements of Inspector Hughes, led me to ask the questions which I felt justified in asking on the floor of this House, and which have at- last brought forth the explanation of the minister to-night.
The minister thought it was in bad taste on my part to refer to Inspector Hughes, because he is now in France fighting for
[Mr. Doherty.! '
his King and country. I have not said one word to reflect in the slightest degree upon Colonel Hughes, a colonel of the militia. If I had any opinion to express of him in that regard, it would have to be favourable, from all I have heard. But I must say that when a man who is an inspector of penitentiaries feels that he has a right, in making a report, to place certain statements in that report reflecting on me as one of the persons who saw fit to ask an explanation, statements which in my judgment are not true, the fact that he is not now in the country is no reason why I should refrain from referring to him. I did not refer to Colonel Hughes, but I did refer to Inspector W. 6. Hughes, and if they happen to be the same person that is no concern of mine. I am not discussing him from a military aspect at all; I believe that he is doing his duty very efficiently and well. But I say that when, as one of the inspectors of penitentiaries, he appended his name to that report, he signed statements which he must have known were untrue and misleading.
In regard to Dr. Phelan, the minister has given reasons why he felt justified in granting him a pension. I have no doubt the minister is perfectly sincere, and thinks that he did right. But, notwithstanding his remarks, I am still of the opinion that I entertained in the first place, that this man Phelan did not conduct himself, while surgeon of the penitentiary at Kingston, in a manner which justified the minister in pensioning him at $1,500 a year. In regard to the language which he used and which will embellish the pages of Hansard to-morrow, I might say that I do not think that is quite all the language employed on that occasion. The minister holds the view that the language was not desirable language, that it did not conform to the dignity of the position the man held; and the only reason I had for referring to it was that the language was, to a certain extent, an index of the man. That, taken in conjunction with other things, led me to believe that this man should not have received the consideration which was accorded to him. In regard to his. suggestion to the witness Redden that he should not speak the truth when he went into the box, I think that if the minister refers to the evidence he will not find exactly the words he quoted to-night. I do not think he will find that Dr. Phelan claimed that he had said this in jest, but he will find that Dr. Phelan did ask this man Redden to go on the witness stand, and, after taking an

oath to tell the truth, the whole truth, deliberately to refrain from telling the truth. I do not know how the minister can get around that, because that is another indication of the character of the man. Taken by itself that might not be sufficient to justify one in condemning the man; but 1 say that is an index of the man's character and disposition. He admits having received some money from men who the minister says were not guards at the time. But that is not the point. Every man who seeks to become a guard has to be examined by the surgeon of the penitentiary, to see whether he is physically fit for that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He may be examined
by the surgeon of the penitentiary.
I understood that even if he had been examined outside, it was one of the duties of the surgeon to pass upon him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The practice is as
stated.

When a man comes in, the practice is to examinfe that man. That is one of the duties the surgeon is supposed to perform without extra remuneration. The fact that he admitted receiving. $4 is neither here nor there. That does not mean that that was all he received; it merely indicates that it was the only case brought up and proved. The commissioners said there was no use in taking up further time with cases of that kind as they considered the charge proved. It is all very well for the minister to say that the surgeon of t}ie penitentiary 'vyas not responsible for the system, that the responsibility should not be placed upon his shoulders, and that his employers are responsible for that system. To a certain extent that is true, but is it not also true that the Minister of Justice, as the head of the department, expects to receive from the surgeons of the various penitentiaries suggestions in regard to improvements along the line of their work. He expects to receive suggestions from chaplains in connection with their work. He gets reports from the surgeons. He is the minister to whom is stated what is required, or what should be done in the way of effecting improvements in the hospital. If he does not get reports from the surgeons of the various penitentiaries pointing out what should be done, how is he to know what is required?
It would be unreasonable to expect a
1.351
lawyer, an ex-judge, a man who has had no medical training, to say what is required in the hospitals or insane wards. What he has a right to expect is that the men in charge of these departments will make suggestions to him as to the improvements that should be made, and the fact remains that the man who was in charge of that department in Kingston penitentiary not only did not make suggestions of improvements, but, in his reports to the minister repeatedly misrepresented the condition of things in the penitentiary in regard to the hospital and insane ward. He not only misrepresented the conditions in his report, but misrepresented the Minister of Justice.
While the minister was speaking with regard to the hospitals, I asked him if he did not think there was room for improvement in the conditions.
10 p.m. He said, " Yes, he thought there was room for considerable improvement in the general conditions, as to cleanliness and so on." But what does this surgeon say in his report to the minister and to the country? He says:
The hospital, as in former years, has been kept immaculate as regards cleanliness and sanitation. The Minister of Justice, when on a visit to this department, expressed his extreme satisfaction with the. methods of its management, the absolute cleanliness of its cells and corridors, and the care and attention given the patients. It would be, indeed, difficult to find anywhere a ward in any public hospital maintained in such a spotless condition, due regard, of course, bein given to the character of the patients and their absolute custody.
Here is a man who says that the Minister of Justice went there and found the hospital fine, and expressed his supreme satisfaction with the 'conditions, and with the cleanliness, while the Minister of Justice, referring to the matter to-day, says- there is room for vast improvement in the genera] conditions, and especially as to cleanliness.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was speaking of what I gathered from the report of the commissioners. I do not recollect that I used that language, but I may |say that, |OB the particular day on which I visited the hospital, it did strike me as being clean. 1 certainly did not make a' speech, and I do not remember that I expressed myself on the subject. When my hon. friend asked me whether there was room for improvement I was speaking of what I had gathered from the general tenor of the commissioners' report. When I visited the hospital, I did not pretend to make a care-

ful scrutiny, but on that particular day it looked clean.

The minister has no recollection of having expressed his extreme satisfaction; had he done so, it would have impressed itself on the cells of his brain and he would have recollected it. I am not charging that the minister did say this; I will take the minister's word.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not say I did not.

It is one of those cases of being on the fence. What I am saying is that the surgeon of that penitentiary makes a report, in which he says that the Minister of Justice expressed extreme satisfaction with the conditions there. What does the commission, appointed by the minister, say in regard to this? We have here the opinion of Dr. Etherington, who was one of the commissioners, in regard to this hospital and its immaculate cleanliness, the hospital that was absolutely spotless, according to the expressed opinion of Dr. Phelan, the hospital of which the sanitation and ventilation were absolutely perfect, and where nothing was to be desired. What do the commissioners say in regard to that? They say:
It is difficult to conceive what characteristics of the building; set apart for the care of the sick at the Kingston penitentiary warrant it being designated " hospital."
Dr. Phelan could not be held responsible for the poor build,ing; that is not the point. They go on to say:
There is nothing in the building or equipment which justifies the name. Some 36 inside cells, inferior in their arrangements to the cells occupied by the healthy prisoners, house those whose Illness is serious enough to make necessary their admission. In these cells there is not effective ventilation.
A direct contradiction of what Dr. Phelan reports to the minister and to the country. The. commissioners further say:
There is not effective ventilation; and save for an obsolete bucket for the excreta, sanitary appliances are absent. The two baths and water-closets are hopelessly out of date. Under no conditions are the patients permitted to have exercise in the fresh air, nor indeed to leave their cells for any purpose.
The operating room (so-called), where serious cases have been, and must he dealt with as they arise, has an old wooden table hut no other equipment:
A fine hospital, everything up to date, according to the report which Dr. Phelan made, and yet in the operating room they had nothing but an old wooden table, no other equipment whatever. The Minister
fMr. Doherty.]
of Justice might never notice anything of that kind:; he would not be expected to notice that sort of thing. As long as he did not find a pile of dirt in the middle of the floor, or some old broken chairs around he would say, " This is fine, this is splendid, this is all right." His knowledge, though vast, though very extensive, though very broad, and though it covers a multitude of things-in this I think it covers a multitude of sins so far as Phelan is concerned-is not adequate to enable him to appreciate the conditions in that hospital, and he might easily be fooled in regard to them. The commissioners say:
When your commissioners visited this room, many old books lay about the floor and the place was not clean.	.
Yet they placed that under the direction of Dr. Phelan. It may be that Dr. Phelan was mat responsible few the muxaJber of square feet in the room, or for the size of the hospital, but I will say that the wildest endeavour to excuse the inefficiency of this man cannot convince us that he was not responsible for the cleanliness of this place or that he should not be held responsible for the fact that there were old books and papers on the floor. The commissioners say:
In all, there was a condition of affairs which should not have been tolerated.
Tolerated by whom? The one man who had it in his power to have this changed was the man who said that everything was all right. .
Again, there is to be noted an all but complete absence of satisfactory records. Inspector Stewart's commendation of the existing conditions can only mean that he is not competent to express an opinion upon this aspect of prison management. Although his annual reports give a different impression, the surgeon in his evidence before the commission stated that many changes were necessary to make the hospital whiat it should be.
I am not basing my contention that Dr. Phelan is not entitled to the superannuation he has received on the one point of language, on the one point of perjury, on the one point of graft, but I am putting all these things together. I say that the most important point is in regard to rule 52. He absolutely disregarded that rule. The evidence shows that he disregarded it. Case after case came before the commission in regard to that rule where it was shown that he made no examination whatever, not even a cursory examination, of prisoners to see if they had any infectious disease. Case after case came before the commission until the commission finally said that there was

no use of introducing further witnesses to establish the fact. We have conclusive evidence that he absolutely disregarded rule 52. As a result of his failure to examine first offenders who came in, tubercular and infected prisoner^ were herded with men who were healthy. That was the state of affairs which this report showed to exist, and it is a state of affairs which would not exist under an efficient surgeon in a penitentiary. The same is true with regard to rule 53, which has to do with hygiene. These are the things that I hold him most responsible for. He was the surgeon of the institution, and as such he was responsible for the diet of the prisoners, he was responsible for seeing that the prisoners obtained exercise in the open air, he was responsible for the ventilation and sanitation of cells in which the prisoners were confined, and he was responsible for the fact that, for a time at least on Sundays, prisoners got their three meals at nine, eleven and one o'clock, and got nothing more until next morning. If the surgeon of the penitentiary had reported to the minister that sick prisoners were having their meals crowded into two or three hours in the day, and that they got nothing to eat until next morning, what do you suppose would have been the result? There is no doubt about the truth of the statement that during all these hours between one p.m. on Sunday until next morning they had nothing to eat, and were confined to their cells without any proper ventilation. If he had called that to the attention of the minister I am sure that condition would have been immediately changed. It is because of these facts that I enter my protest against Dr. Phelan being accorded the treatment he has received in so far as his pension is concerned. It will not make any difference, he will get his pension just the same, and he will go on practising his profession in Kingston. I hope he does well, but he will have to do better when he is dealing with the general public in Kingston than he did when he was dealing with the prisoners at Portsmouth or he will need every dollar that the Government has so kindly bestowed upon him.
Mr. ARTHUR B. COPP (Westmorland): I am sure we are all very much interested, and a little shocked, to hear the charges made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in regard to the conduct of affairs at Kingston penitentiary. I know how dangerous it is to interfere with family quarrels, and therefore I do not intend to
intervene in this quarrel or disagreement between the hon. member for Frontenac and the hon. Minister of Justice. The hon. member for Frontenac has made some very serious charges regarding the conduct of the Kingston penitentiary. He has confined his remarks largely to this institution, but he has also given some attention to the conditions at Stony Mountain. It does not matter to me whether the hon. member for Frontenac is correct or not in regard to the superannuation of Dr. Phelan by the Justice Department. As I understand, he has been superannuated, he is drawing his allowance, he will continue to draw it, and nothing that can be said or done here will change the situation in regard to that. But, it seems to me that the strongest condemnation uttered by the hon. member for Frontenac had to do with the conditions that may arise in all the penitentiaries throughout the Dominion in regard to the reports of the inspectors who have a very great deal to do with these institutions. The hon. member for Frontenac has charged that the inspectors have made false reports to the minister in regard to these institutions. That is a very serious charge and one which must be admitted by every hon. member who has anything to do with public affairs or with these institutions in which unfortunates are confined either ias prisoners or insane convicts. The Minister of Justice rather intimates that nothing should be said in regard to one of the inspectors who made a report in regard to one of these institutions, as he is now at the front. I have nothing to say in regard to that gentleman-I do not know him personally, and I am sure that I would be one of the last to cast any reflections upon his character or reputation in regard to the matter. But the charge is made by an hon. member of this House that this officer has made a false report to the Minister of Justice in regard to the Kingston Penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I would not be differing from the hon. member for Frontenac if I pointed out that, while the hon. member for Frontenac says that the statements in this report are false and unsustained, the report of the inspectors is in the nature of an answer to the report of the Royal Commission that was appointed to carry on the investigation, and which Royal Commission took evidence. The difference between the two reports consists in a different appreciation, by the Royal Commissioners on the one side and by the penitentiary inspectors on the other, of the results

of the evidence. It is hardly a matter of an issue of fact as between them. It is true they differ about questions of fact, but they are dealing with facts established by the evidence. One says the evidence proves this and the otheT says that it proves something else. However, the minister has the evidence before him. It is not a question of veracity about a specific fact on the part of the inspectors. They may be wrong in their appreciation of the evidence and the Royal Commissioners may he right. I do not understand the issue to be as to an absolute misstatement in the report of a fact known to an individual.

I am very gl-a,d to hear the minister's explanation, if it may be called such, of the difference between the Royal Commission and the Penitentiary Commission. But I was referring more particularly to the charge made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards.' that the inspectors had made a false report in regard to the conditions. That is a serious charge, whether it b,e true or not; the question of veracity may rest between the two commissions, or between the hon. member for Frontenac and the Minister of Justice. What I say is that it is a very serious charge for an hon. member to make, unless he can back it up with facts. The hon. member for Frontenac says that a commission was appointed'-I presume by the Minister of Justice-consisting of G. M. Macdondll, Dr. Etherington, and J. P. Downey, and he claimed that that commission was no good, that they were not worth fifteen cents a day. My hon. friend is getting in a dangerous zone when he has the temerity to criticise a commission appointed by this Government. A few days ago -when hon. gentlemen on this side of the House ventured to suggest a Royal Commission might not give the exact attention to public matters that we thought desirable, we were branded as disloyal, and as forgetting the duty of members of this House. How dared we suggest that a commission would do anything but what was right and proper? But to-night rwe have the hon. member for Frontenac, for years a prominent and loyal supporter of this Administration, making these very serious charges 'against the Government; and all the more serious because he does not want to find fault with this Administration, of which he is such 'a loyal supporter. But his conscience forces him to do it, on behalf of the poor 'unfortunates in our penitentiaries.
fair. Doherty.]
Their voice cannot be heard; they are behind the iron doors, and, if we are to believe the hon. member, are treated in a most inhumane way by their keepers. It seems to me that the duty devolves upon the minister to appoint, if necessary, another royal commission to inquire whether the charges made by the hon. member for Frontenac are true. I care nothing about Dr. Phelan; that question is a mere bagatelle. But what I do care about is that the unfortunates in our penitentiaries from the Atlantic to the Pacific shall not be treated in the inhumane way that has been described in Kingston. I think a very grave responsibility rests upon the Minister of Justice to ascertain whether there is any truth in the charges made by the hon. member for Frontenac against the officials of Kingston penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When we were discussing these matters to-day, we were discussing things that had happened; we were talking about the past. It is not suggested, as I understand it, that there is any ill-treatment of prisoners at the present day. At all events, I have not heard any such charges, and I try to keep myself as well informed as I possibly can.

We hear a great many complaints. I understand, of course, that it is easy to make complaints. These unfortunates are naturally dissatisfied, and not of the very best class of citizens, and that must be taken into consideration when considering these complaints. I hear quite a number of complaints in regard to the Maritime penitentiary, which is situated in my county. I do not say that these complaints are grievous, but it is well to take care that they do not grow; we do not want the same conditions there as prevailed at Kingston.
If it is true, as the hon. member for Frontenac charges, that the inspectors are not carrying out their duties in a proper manner, what guarantee has the Minister of Justice that the same conditions do not prevail in other penitentiaries throughout the country?
