The Minister of Justice tonight in defending his department led me to believe that he was very sincere in his statements; almost tender-hearted in fact, to the penitentiary officials. While there might be little things here and there, he found it very hard to harden his heart and dismiss these men. I gathered that if he erred at all, it would be on the humane side.

The hon. member for Frontenac has found fault with the large superannuation allowance paid to Dr. Phelan. In my own county, in the Dorchester penitentiary, there is a man whom I have known for a number of years. He was the chief keeper, and is in the very prime of life, being no more than forty-five years old, if that. An investigation was held with regard to this man. I cannot say who conducted the investigation, but I had occasion to read the evidence. At the time this investigation was held, I had been in politics in my province for some fifteen years, and had never up to that time had the slightest idea whether this man was a Liberal or a Conservative.
He was a good official, a young, bright, energetic, capable man, eminently qualified to fill any such position as that which hb held. The gravamen of the charge against him was that he had picked up a newspaper-and it happened to be a Liberal newspaper, published in the city of St. John-and apparently it was against the rules to read a newspaper within certain hours. But the newspaper came in and he picked it up. It was reported to the Justice Department that this man had broken one of the rules of the institution. An investigation was held, and the man was retired on a gratuity of $1,985, which he had earned by his service of twenty-one years, eight months and, seven days in office. After his case had been investigated he was told that unless he resigned he would be dismissed and forced out on the streets with nothing. He resigned and took the gratuity from the Government. I say confidently and without fear of successful contradiction, I care not 'from whom, that there was no reasonable charge made against this man. It was found that he was a Liberal, and his head was demanded by the Conservatives of my county, and the Minister of Justice, in spite of his humane ideas, hardened, Ms heart and cutxoff that man's official head, even though, as he tells us, he could not do it in the case of 'the man in Kingston.

I might point out to my
hon. friend that the gentleman at Kingston was also a Liberal.

That does not make it any better or .worse. But when the minister attempts to defend his department against the charges made by my hon. friend, from Frontenac and tries to convince us that he has been influenced by humane motives, I
merely put before the committee the fact that in the case of this man in my county be turned him out with a gratuity of less than two thousand dollars, though I defy any one to show that Leonard Hutchinson was not a useful, capable official. I do not know whether the inspectors held an investigation in that ease or not. But if the inspectors are simply the political creatures of the department, to go about the country and make false reports, as charged by the hon. member for Frontenac, these reports should not be considered or acted upon by the minister. If these things have occurred in Dorchester penitentiary, no doubt other things of the same kind have occurred in other penitentiaries. Let the minister come out openly and state his position. If he is going to take politics into his department and dismiss officials that are opposed to him politically, let him say so, and we shall know where we stand. Here was a man who had given twenty-one years of good service in this institution, and had worked his way up from the position of guard to that of chief keeper; yet to suit the whim and fancy of some individuals his head was cut off. I put it to the minister, who tells us of his soft heart and his tender conscience, whether it was not a pretty small piece of business to discharge in this way the man who had spent so many years in the service of the department over which he presides. He tells us that he wished Dr. Phelan to get justice, he having been for some years in the employ of the department. I know nothing of that case; but if it would have been a hardship to Dr. Phelan to be turned adrift, it was equally a hardship in the case of this man in Westmorland county. The minister not only drove him out of the penitentiary, but he drove him out of the province. We are paying handsomely to bring immigrants into our province, but the minister drives out men who are worth far more than any immigrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
pleading of the case of Leonard Hutchinson does definite credit to his capacity for clothing a case in affecting and pathetic language. But it also reveals the fact that the hon. gentleman is utterly and entirely misinformed as to the facts. I never heard what Mr. Hutchinaoin's politics were until the hon. gentleman informed us to-night that he was a Liberal. No one outside the penitentiary ever made complaint about Mr. Hutehin-

son, but it was claimed by officials in the penitentiary that he was guilty, not only of the offence of bringing in a newspaper on one occasion, but of very grave insubordination, as was clearly and distinctly proven. I do not quite grasp what reproach is made to me. I might have dismissed that man and so made him lose his gratuity; but, with the soft-heartedness for which the hon. gentleman gives me credit, I gave him the opportunity to resign, so that he got his gratuity. The hon. gentleman tries to make a contrast between the case of Dr. Phelan and that of this gentleman. Dr. Phelan got what he got under the law, just as Mr. Hutchinson did. I think that when the hon. gentleman ascertains the real facts -and he can see the reports if he wishes to see them-he will find that there was no trace of political partisanship from start to finish. I am blamed for being too good to the Liberals, and on the other hand I am blamed for not being good enough to them. It has been pointed out that Dr. Phelan is a Liberal, as we are told Mr. Hutchinson is also. Dr. Phelan came in at a time when he could secure a pension under the law, and he had been paying two per cent of his salary all along in order to have his superannuation; but Mr. Hutchinson, at most, was entitled only to a gratuity. As I say, I greatly admire the hon. gentleman's eloquence in putting his case, but when he knows the facts, I am sure he will see that Mr. Hutchinson had no injustice to complain of.

I am much obliged to the
hon. minister for the information he has given me, but that does not settle the matter. Maybe I know more about this matter than he thinks I do. Does he want this committee, or does he want me, to believe that when a man's dismissal is desired a letter is written to the department stating that the man is a Grit and demanding his official head?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I had not any correspondence of that kind.

That is exactly what I say. He will not get correspondence of that kind; but from the action he took in dismissing Mr. Hutchinson it is quite evident he understood the correspondence whether he received it from the officials of his department	or from	anybody	else.
The officials who laid charges against Mr. Hutchinson were Conservative officials who did not want him there. The inspectors and other officials in my hon. friend's
fMr. Doherty.]
department listened to these representations, and an investigation was held which proved that the charges were of a very trivial character indeed. I have read the evidence, and my hon. friend cannot make the people in that locality, not even his own friends, believe that there was no politics in connection with the dismissal of [Mr. Leonard Hutchinson. I know whereof I speak; I know something about the correspondence, something about the evidence, something about the affidavits that were made with regard to Leonard Hutchinson's politics. The' investigation was held with no other intention, irrespective of the evidence, than that of securing Mr. Hutchinson's resignation or dismissal. When Mr. Hutchinson was told what would happen to him if he did not resign, he took, my hon. friend's advice and did resign, to save the few hundred dollars that were doled out to him for the benefit of his wife and family for the next 25 years of his life, if he lives that long. This is his reward for' the true and loyal service that he gave the department for 21 odd years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may know all about things in that locality, but I know just what happened in the place where it Was decided to dismiss the gentleman, and just on what evidence it was done. I do not know what people were saying down in that locality; that had nothing to do with it. I made the decision, I made it on the evidence, without knowledge of what Mr. Hutchinson's politics were, and entirely without knowledge of all the things that the hon. gentleman does know-that is, of the things that were being said in that locality.

I am sorry to hear the Minister of Justice say that he takes the full responsibility of the dismissal of Leonard Hutchinson from the position that he held in the Dorchester .penitentiary. Ilf ever there was a true, loyal and faithful servant, .it was Leoenard Hutchinson. I know whereof I speak; I have been there.
Oh, oh.

I am very glad indeed that my hon. friends have something to take their minds off the seriousness of the charges made by the hon. member for Frontenac in regard to the Kingston penitentiary. Their faces have been very long this afternoon and evening, and I am glad that something relieves them from the ten-

sion they have been under during this discussion. I have been at Dorchester penitentiary many times. The hon. member for Rimouski this afternoon referred to the fact that we have no French officials in Dorchester penitentiary; I know the officials who are there, and splendid officials they are. I am sorry that the hon. minister, holding the high position that he does, should, for the sake of satisfying a few friends down in that locality, dismiss Mr. Hutchinson from office and pay him nearly $2,000 to get him out of the way for the sake of helping one of his political friends to an office which he could not get unless Mr. Hutchinson was out of the way.

Mr. Hutchinson, was
appointed over twenty-one years ago, by a Conservative Government.
Is not the fact that he has been in the service over twenty-one years all the more reason why he should be given consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
said that I had dismissed him because he was a Liberal.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon, I said nothing of the kind. I said that my hon. friend dismissed him for no other purpose than to please some of his political friends in that locality.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is no doubt convinced of what he is saying, but he has never made a statement more absolutely untrue than that there was any motive of that kind in connection with the dismissal of Mr. Hutchinson. I am the man who dismissed him, upon the evidence that was before me, showing that he had been guilty of insubordination. That, in my judgment, called for his dismissal. Perhaps every one in that locality is saying the things to which my hon. friend refers, but I want to put myself on record as to the fact in that particular matter. I know the fact and the other hon. gentleman does not.

When the hon. minister tells me that he did this without taking Mr. Hutchinson's politics into consideration, then I do not wonder that the hon. member for Frontenac questions the administration of the affairs of the Justice Department. I know the schemes that were laid to bring these charges against Leonard Hutchinson. I know the plotting that was done, the arrangements that were made, the caucuses
that were held to get a charge against him.
If my hon. friend does not know that, he is not as shrewd as I take him to be. There must be something; he must have smelt a rat, if I may use a slang expression, in regard to the dismissal of Mr. Hutchinson.

The hon. member foi Frontenac has made the allegation, in setr terms, that the inspectors of the Justice Department do not deal justly with the affairs of that position, and that, in consequence, wrong has been done. That is to say, the minister is depending on officials who do not deal honestly by the business that is placed in their charge, and for that reason he becomes, as is alleged by the hon. member for Frontenac, a party to what is other than justice. That is exactly what the hon. member for Westmorland asserts.
I have not troubled the House or the Government very much with complaints about such transactions in my own constituency, but I must say that there was a transaction in connection with the wardenship of the penitentiary in my own constituency that bears out exactly the contention that has been made. I do not suggest that the Minister of Justice would use his high position for merely political purposes knowing that he was doing so. But, having heard the remarks of the hon. member for Frontenac and the hon. member for Westmorland, my opinion is that those upon whom he has depended for his information have deliberately and intentionally misrepresented the conditions to him, leaving him to take a course not in accordance with justice and not in accordance with the best interests of the administration of the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a very grave charge. As I understand the statement of the hon. member for Frontenac, it is that the report of the commissioners to the minister, for publication, was not true.
That is it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That report, as I have pointed, out, rests on the commissioners' appreciation of certain evidence, and is written, not as a statement of particular fact to be reported to the minister, but as their conclusions as to the facts established by certain evidence. That evidence itself was before tbte minister, and there was likewise before the minister a report of a Royal Commission which reached different conclusions on the same evidence. My hon. friend suggested that that raises a question of veracity between the Royal

Commission on one hand and the inspectors and the hon. member for Frontenac on the other. I think we are a little at cross purposes. They take a different view of what was proved on a particular occasion, and each argue their view of it. It is a veTy serious charge, as the hon. member for Edmonton will recognize, against the inspector, and if either the hon. member for Westmorland or the hon. member for Edmonton is prepared to put before me anything in the nature of evidence to establish that charge I shall certainly most carefully look into it. If, on doing so, I find that there is conclusive evidence to prove such a charge, I shall be grateful to the hon. gentleman for calling attention to it.
Mr. OLIVER^ I have not brought this matter to the attention of the minister on my own account. I merely say that, taking the argument of the hon. member for Frontenac, accepting his assertions as true, I am bound to reach the conclusion that the action taken was taken because of improper representations made for improper purposes, for purposes aside from the public interest. But I am not taking action in the matter and do not desire to take action. While the minister argues that there is no question of veracity against the penitentiary commissioners as alleged by the hon. member for Frontenac, let me say that these penitentiary commissioners are the men upon whose reports the minister bases his action in the large majority of oases. In the particular case mentioned, he found that the opinions of these penitentiary commissioners were opposed by a Royal Commission. I suppose that they did not agree with the views of the minister in that case. But had there been no Royal 'Commission, had there been nothing to check the report made by these penitentiary commissioners, would not the minister have been misled in that case? On the face of it, a manifest injustice appears to have been done in the case I referred to. Being satisfied that these commissioners have reported erroneously and intentionally erroneously to the minister in the case mentioned by the hon. member for Frontenac,
I am bound to suppose that they did so in the Edmonton case of which I spoke. I quite agree that the charge is a most serious one, and I put it before the minister, not with the intention of attacking him in any way. The administration of his department ultimately comes back to- him. He is 
absolutely responsible for tblaft administration,' and it is no final or satisfactory answer to say: I acted on the report of my officers. In the end it .must be carried beyond that, and the minister is responsible for the character of the report his cdmmis-sioners make. It would not be doing justice to the minister, after having heard the definite statements and the .strong position taken by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), not to inform him that, on the face of the case at Edmonton, the suggestions of the hon. member for Frontenac were well supported and well warranted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In regard to the case
of Hutchinson, my action was not on the mere report of an inspector; the sworn evidence was before me. As to the case at Edmonton I cannot say.
Who held that investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my memory serves
me it was Inspector Hughes, but the depositions came to me.
Did the inspector make a report in regard to the dismissals?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I presume there was a report, but on a matter that turns on a question of fact I always read the evidence.
I do not doubt that; but is it not a fact that there was a report pertaining to the dismissals?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no doubt thert was.
After reading the evidence you acted on the report and the evidence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. <
But the investigation was held by an officer of your department, and a report was made to you by one of the inspectors, to the effect -that Hutchinson be dismissed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, with the evidence.

What is the actual population of the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, and are there any statistics- showing -the particular causes of crime? Is the greater proportion of that crime due to the abuse of liquor?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The actual population is about 450.
Is there a decrease for the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think there has been an increase in the last fiscal year. We have in the -whole penitentiary population an increase of about sixty or seventy, and there is a small increase in St. Vincent de Paul.

In view of the importance of the debate which took place the other day on the question of prohibition, would the minister inform the House whether the principal cause of crime, taking all the penitentiaries, is the abuse of liquor? I mention this because my brother, who is the sheriff of Montreal, happened to study that question in the Montreal jail at Bordeaux. He sent a letter to the hon. member for Bonaventure the other day saying how appalling was the effect of liquor in respect of crime. He says that in the jail at Bordeaux, where there are generally from 400 to 600 inmates, the real cause of the large number of imprisonments is liquor. I would like the minister to state to the House, for the information of the public and of the members, if, as a matter of fact, liquor is not the supreme cause of crime in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The last report on penitentiaries shows that in St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary in 1914, the total number of inmates was 401, of whom 207 are classified as intemperate, and 194 as temperate.
I understand, that these statistics rest merely upon the statements of the convicts themselves. The only means we have of ascertaining in the penitentiaries whether ,an inmate is temperate or intemperate is his own statement.
I thought that, when every prisoner was sent to a penitentiary, there was a report from the judge mentioning his antecedents.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, all that comes to us is the committal showing the date of the trial, the offence of which the prisoner is convicted, and the length of the sentence. When the convict comes 'in he is questioned, and I understand that the statistics, of the kind to which I have referred, rest upon the statement the convicts make. In the Remission branch, we do get a certain amount of information in the judge's report with regard to the habits of the prisoners when application is made to release them, but in the penitentiary records there is nothing to show what their habits have been except the information -which is collected in the way I have described.
-Can the minister ascertain in a general way from his officer whether the real cause of crime is not due to the abuse of liquor?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall communicate with the wardens and see to what extent they are prepared to express an opinion on that question. I think that that would be the only way to get the information. The wardens, or the penitentiary surgeons might be .able to give us some light, but they would have to rely on the prisoners' statements. I think the reports of the criminal courts would afford a better means of getting the information.

I thought that the department had criminal statistics showing
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The statistics purport to show who are intemperate and who are temperate, and, they show that 11 p.m. a great majority are, on their own confession, intemperate
people.

Has the minister maintained the excellent practice of allowing the Salvation Army to receive prisoners when they are released? Some years ago a predecessor of my hon. friend, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, I think, permitted the Salvation Army to send representatives to the gates of the penitentiaries. I know that they go to the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, and I presume the practice is carried out elsewhere? The prisoners, when they come out, are received by the representatives of the Salvation Army, who give them the glad and, helping hand. I would like to know if that practice has been maintained, because I think that the Salvation Army has rendered most valuable service in that regard to our prisoners. If my hon. friend has not maintained it I would ask him to do so. In our large cities the Salvation Army are doing wonderful work, and, no better institution could be found to help the prisoners when they leave the penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In many cases the Salvation Army representatives do take charge of the prisoners, more particularly those released on leave, and we have always been happy to continue the relations that were established, I think through thfe parole officer, and to avail ourselves of their assist-

ance. But, while the work of the Salvation Army is exceedingly valuable, there are other societies who do work of that kind, and we are always glad to have the co-operation of these societies.
I understood, my hon. friend to say that in dealing with the evidence that came before him in regard to the case of Hutchinson he did not know what his politics were.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no recollection that his politics appeared on the face of it.
The minister has not the slightest doubt that the inspector who made the report recommending Hutchinson's dismissal would know about his politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not ask him; I really do not know whether he would or not. I cannot answer my hon. friend's question.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I heard a moment ago, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) asking of the Minister of Justice what is the chief determinant of crime in most cases? You will allow me, Sir, to make -a reiply from a full knowledge of the question. For the last ten years I have been acting as crown attorney in Montreal, I am quite familiar with what hakes place at the criminal assizes, at summary trials and in the police courts. I moreover, as a royal commissioner, had to investigate in 1897 conditions existing in St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. At that time I looked up the docket of every convict to find out the grounds for his conviction. I say without hesitation that in the majority of cases, the primary cause was drunkenness, as is the case in all convictions, at the assizes or the lower courts. I am now convinced that mostly all crimes may be traced back to the drinking habit. During the last term, ending yesterday, 150 cases came up 'before the Montreal courts. I had to examine those cases very closely and with very few exceptions, the abuse of liquor was the main instigator of crimes. During this last term, men were condemned for manslaughter, the result of speeding at the hands of intemperate drivers. Take forgery: as a rule a man who has not lost his wits, will not deliberately commit this infamous and awful crime. And what about arson? When you ask those who have set 	.
fire to their neighbour's house or bam what prompted them to do so, you get a reply something like the following: "Well, we went to law together and I lost my case; I went on a spree and in a spirit of revenge, I set fire to the building." That is a sample of the explanation commonly given everywhere. And now, how does a man become a murderer or a burglar? Generally the prime mover is liquor. Quarrels, grievous assaults always follow drunkenness. I intend my words as a reply to the hon. member for Rouville and likewise for the hon. the Minister of Justice. It is easy to find out when a prisoner- is addicted to drinking. Their confessions are not our only criterion, we have their -pedigree. The old offenders are well known. The habitual frequenters of police courts are easily recognized by the provincial police and also by the constables of Montreal and surrounding towns. Their habits are always noted in their jail-entry and penal certificate, and on their being bronght back to the court, we produce their docket to see whether they are of intemperate or temperate habits; and in every file at St. Vincent de Paul or Bordeaux, the convicts' habitual behaviour is noted by the magistrate who has sentenced the prisoners. The general conduct of each individual prisoner is noted. If they are unknown to the officers, an investigation is held by the police and detectives in order to find out the general behaviour of those convicts. That information also reveals the fact that with very few exceptions drinking is the chief cause of crime. It is easy to get the pedigree of prisoners who are brought before police or criminal courts. A man is always known in his town or village and if he is addicted ito strong drink, the fact is notorious.
I take as example the parish in which it has been my privilege to live for the last thirty years; there is not a man whose general habits are not common knowledge Every one in a locality knows when fa man is temperate and if he is intemperate, the people know it even more readily.
A mistake becomes impossible. When a man is arrested, if it is required to find out what were his antecedents with Tegard to the use of spirits, you have only to ask his neighbour and you can find out. However, I just cannot but state right here that an improvement is taking place. I have noticed that for three or four years past, the indulgence in strong drink is de-

creasing, even gradually dying out. The courts have to deal more nowadays with cases of fraud. Hard times, poverty, commercial, and industrial stringency all tend to increase fraudulent dealings considerably. A large number of people are hard pressed; they have gone into speculative transactions that have turned to their disadvantage; they^put up a lot- of money and lost all. Many even among professional men, have unfortunately made themselves liable to arrest. Busiuess stress and difficulties have caused new misdemeanours.
Mr. Chairman, while we are discussing the Estimates tor penitenitaries, I will call to the minister's especial notice the defective classing of convicts in penitentiaries. It must be deplored that young people convicted for the first time, perhaps for a serious offence, should be sentenced and confined indiscriminately with old criminals, thieves and even murderers, old offenders for the most part who become dangerous company for those younger prisoners.	.
In 1897, when we had to report on the conditions in St. Vincent de Paul, there was inserted a very special recommendation that a special department be set apart for young prisoners. How can it be expected that a young, man after entering a penitentiary for a couple of years will be able to reform when be is thrown in' the company of professional crooks? They are forever lost.	.
If the Department of Justice saw to setting apart in the penitentiary a special department for those new convicts, they might be amenable to reform and turned into good citizens. I took every occasion under the old administration to suggest that classification, which however was not made. The Minister of Justice would be well serving society in segregating those who. are convicted for the first time away from old criminals. The minister cannot be too strongly impressed of the importance of the benefit he would confer in acting along the lines I suggest. Quite often, courts and crown attorneys are loath to send those prisoners to a penitentiary on that account, because we realize that there is a chance of their becoming worse instetad of improving.
A word now as to a certain class of criminals. There are men in the penitentiary who make a profession of passing their lives in prison. As soon as they are discharged, their chief aim is to be brought hack and
convicted so as to pursue within the walls of the penitentiary their disastrous and immoral work. I know very well whereof I speak and such has been my observation during my thirty-five years at the Bar and ten years as crown attorney. I therefore plead that everything he earnestly done to carry out that suggestion; in the name of humanity I ask that the segregation of first offenders be brought about.
Does the minister receive a report from the juvenile courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think we receive any report from juvenile courts. They are provincial institutions.

I know, hut I thought
that the minister received a report on their work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think so. It has not come to my personal notice. I will look into it.	s

Will the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue explain the increase?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. L. PATENAUDE (Minister of Inland Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, at the session which ended in April or May, 1915, Parliament decided to amend the Act concerning the Adulteration of Foodstuffs so as to cover the sale of maple sugar and syrup in Canada.
The amendments were enacted in proper time and all those interested in that industry admit they ought to be beneficial. The expected results possibly aTe not yet apparent, but it must be taken into account that the law has hardly been introduced and that some months must be allowed to pass before a full test is made of its efficiency.
At any rate the provisions of the Act are of great benefit to the farming community, since the manufacturers of pure maple sugar are mostly farmers.
The hon. member for 'Champlain (Mr. Blondin), the then Minister of Inland Revenue, must be given his share of credit for what he brought about, and I feel that his successor in office will show the same spirit and see to it that the law is fully enforced.
On the 29th of February last, some 600 producers of pure maple sugar and syrup attended the annual convention at Rigaud and among other resolutions the following was passed with a proviso for having it transmitted to the Government. I hope
the hon. minister will allow me to read it.
Excerpt from the minutes of the third convention of the Go-operative Society of the Producers of Pure Maple Sugar and Syrup held at Rigaud on Tuesday, February 20, 1916:-
Be it resolyed that notwithstanding the Act passed hy the Parliament of Canada in session assembled in the month of April, 1915, by which was prohibited the imitation of maple products, it is found, as stated in bulletin No. 324 of the Department of Inland Revenue that,out of 234 samples of sugar examined, 204 were found unadulterated, 5 complied with the requirements of the law and 25 were adulterated. The examination of a second set of samples, as reported in bulletin No. 243, found 192 unadulterated, 4 complying with the legal requirements and 43 adulterated;
Moreover that under the name of "Maple-ine " was advertised for sale in the Montreal Star on October 14, 1915, January 25, 1916, February 2 and 24, 1916, an extract for the preparation of Maple syrup;
That therefore this convention while assuring the Government of its appreciation of the enactment of the provisions of 1915 insist on the Act being strictly enforced through exercising greater care to bring to account all trespassers.	,
Jos H. Lefebvre, Secretary.
Rigaud, February 29, 1916.	*
My object in voicing in tbis House the complaint of the convention, is not to bring home to the Department of Inland Revenue any neglect of duty on its part; on the contrary, as I shall prove in a few minutes, the department is to be congratulated on its endeavours to see that the law is carried out. But I only wish to call to the notice of the minister the carelessness of persons who in certain quarters ought to comply with the law like the rest of us. The Act is of general application and nobody is exempted from its operation; the Government cannot therefore set up two standards for exacting compliance with its provisions without thereby endangering the effectiveness of the reform which was brought about. What, then, are the provisions which came into force on the 15th day of April, 1915, being chap. 9, sec. 29 A:-
29a. No person shall manufacture for sale, keep for sale, offer or expose for sale, or sell, any article of food resembling or being an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup, or which is composed partly of maple sugar or maple syrup, and which is not pure maple sugar or pure maple syrup.
2.	Any maple sugar or maple syrup which is not up to the standard prescribed by the sixth schedule to this Act, or, if such standard is changed by the Governor in Council, to such standard as the Governor in Council may from time to time prescribe, shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of this Act.

3.	The word "maple" shall not be used, either alone or in combination with any other word or words, or letter or letters, on the label or other mark, illustration or device on a package containing any article of food, or on any article of food itself, which is not pure maple sugar or pure maple syrup, and any article of food labelled or marked in violation of this subsection shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of this Act.
31.	Every person who willfully adulterates any article of food or any drug, or orders any other person so to do, shall
(a) if such adulteration is, within the meaning of this Act, deemed to be injurious to health, for a first offence, incur a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars and costs, or six months' - Imprisonment, or both, and not less than fifty dollars and costs; and for each subsequent offence, a penalty not exceeding one thousand dollars and costs, or one year's imprisonment, or both, and not less than one hundred dollars and costs;
(&) if such adulteration is, within the meaning of this Act, deemed not to be injurious to health, incur a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs, or three months imprisonment, or both, and not less than twenty-five dollars and costs, and for each subsequent offence, a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars and costs, or six months' imprisonment, or both, and not less .than one hundred dollars and costs.
32.	Every person who, by himself or his agent, sells, offers for sale, or exposes for sale, any article of food Or. any drug which is adulterated within the meaning of this Act shall
(a)	if such adulteration is, within th3 meaning of this Act, deemed to be injurious to health, for the first offence incur a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs or three months' imprisonment, or both and not less than fifty dollars and costs, and for each subsequent offence a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars and costs, or six months imprisonment, or both, and not less than fifty dollars and costs;	.
(b)	if such adulteration is within the meaning of this Act, deemed not to be injurious to health, incur, for the first offence, a penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars and costs, or three months in jail, or both, and not less than twenty-five dollars and costls, and for each subsequent offence a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs, or six months in jail, or both and not less than fifty dollars and costs.
3.	Section 37 of the said Act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
37. Every person who knowingly attaches to any article of food or any drug any label which falsely describes the article sold, or offered or exposed for sale, or who neglects or refuses to label or mark any article of food or drug in accordance with the requirements of this Act shall incur a penalty for the first offence not exceeding two hundred dollars and not less than twenty-five dollars or two months in jail, or both, and for each subsequent offence a penalty not exceeding three hundred dollars and not less than fifty dollars, or four months in jail, or both.
4.	Section 40 of the said Act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:

40. Under such regulations as may be made by the minister, an amount not exceeding one-half of the penalties imposed and recovered under this Act may be. paid to any person who has given information or otherwise aided in' effecting the recovery of the penalty, and the other portion of the penalty shall be paid to the Minister of Finance, and shall form part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
It is easily seen that the Act, which may be improved later on, leaves, as it stands, few loopholes for adulteration. It prohibits entirely the use of the word " maple " in the designation of -any compounded or other syrup which is not the pure maple product. That prohibition -concerning the use of the word " maple " -extends of -course to any label and advertisement of whatever kind.
It follows that a newspaper advertisement of a " mapleine " product constitutes an infringement of the Act and makes the publisher liable to the penalties enacted therein.
The producers of sugar and syrup must not then be taken as complaining wrongly against the Montreal Star of October 14, 1915, January 25, 1916, February 2 and 25, 1916, for publishing in bold type the advertisement of the -Good-win firm- for " Mapleine " to manufacture maple syrup, at 15 cents, 25 -cents and 45 cents a bottle.
It cannot be ag-ain said that such an advertisement is in- its intent and actual working a clear -case' of infringement of the law and of the protection which it was its purpose to -afford to the producers of the genuine article -and to the consumers. And the worst feature of it is not in the advertisement; the inside recipe -tells clearly how -to make a quart, a gallon-, etc., of maple syrup.
I am glad to point out however that the department has already put its ban on this compound, -as may be seen -by the letters I shall now bring to your n-oti-ce.

I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 27th October, and in reply must state that if the articles labelled "Mapleine" are not maple sugar and syrup, both perfectly pure, the word "Mapleine" must be left out, or else it constitutes a violation of both the spirit and letter of the adulteration act relating to maple syrup and sugar.
Tours truly,
(Sig.) P. E. Blondin.
I am ready to acknowledge bow good were the intentions of the Minister of Inland Revenue; yet I find that the " extract of Mapleine " is still for sale, as may be seen by this sample which was 'bought on January 14, 1916, that is 15 months later than the minister's letter, as well as by the advertisements which I have just mentioned offering that article for sale. With those facts brought to his notice I am sure the minister will see to putting a stop to the illegal practice.
Is the sugar industry such as to warrant our taking strict measures to ensure its development? I have no hesitation in saying we should do all in our power along those lines and I am sure I have the indulgence of the House in shortly expounding the outlook for the industry, as it is such as must induce the government to provide as much as in its power lies for the development of this. national industry, and the greatest inducement for our giving the matter serious consideration is the fact that this vast industry presents a vast field of development still unexploited. What I mean by a vast field of development is the magnitude of the area of maple forests in-Canada and particularly in Quebec as -compared with the very -small number of m-aple trees now worked -every spring.
The report goes that Canada has 55,000 sugarmen or people capable of producing maple sugar or syrup.
Of this incredible number, it has been established that -one thousand at the utmost are equipped -in a modern way for production. Suppose those 55,000 owners were to
work only ten acres each of -maple -bush, we should reach the splendid -area of 550,000 acres of maple bushes under exploitation. If we are right in estimating 100 trees to the acre, we reach a total of 55,000,000 trees. And just for the purpose of reasoning if we go on with our computation, we -may accept the statement of experts who state that a tree of ordinary size will yield enough sap to make two pounds of sugar, though some aTe found to yield more and seldom any to yield less. That would mean a total production of 110,000,000 pounds of sugar, which at 10 cents a pound, would net the splendid sum of $11,000,000. The province of Quebec alone would account for $7,150,000, since it produces 65 per cent of the actual output, and 35,000 of the 55,000 sugarmen found in the official census live in the province of Quebec.
I am willing for the -sake of -argument to cut -the figure in two and work from an average t>f 5 acres for each farmer or sugar bush -owner. The result would show 250 miles of bush, 55,000,000 pounds of suga^ valued at $5,500,000, with 5,500,000 gallons of syrup of equal value. Yet the total output of maple products in 1914 could be valued at $2,000,000. The census of 1910 fixed the figure for the province of Quebec at $1,680,000.
Now let us, for the sake of illustration, confine our di-scussion to a smaller area. The counties of 'Soulanges and Vaudreuil have in their area 459 sugar bushes or owners of sugar bushes. Of these 286 are in Vaudreuil and 173 in Soulanges. Yet I am not far from the truth when I state that at least 25 per cent of those bushes are not worked.	,
At the time of the census in 1910, -the output from the maple industry was estimated at $20,681.70 in Vaudreuil, -and $6,253.60 in iSoulanges. I Already had occasion to state that in 1914, 128 farmers of Vaudreuil obtained from the sugar and syrup crop $15,000, -quite a fair amount.
If we surveyed the area -in Vaudreuil where we account for 286 bushes and took it that each bush was worked to the extent of 10 -acres, then a-s figured out above there would be forthcoming -from the crop $57,200, that is $37,000 more than the census of 1910 -and, $42,000 more than the report of 1914. $57,200 for three week's work would average more than the dairy industry in six months. *
The county of Soulanges which has an area of 173 sugar bushes would share to the amount of $34,600 while the census of 1910

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
estimates the output at barely $6,200; figures which must justify us in concluding that in a small area such as those two united counties, the sugar crop would yield from $90,000 to $100,000 for three week's work at the utmost. With such statistics before us, which are subject to slight flue-tuations, are we not forced to admit that the sugar industry is more [profitable than any other branch of farming, even the dairy industry?
There is yet another aspect which must not be overlooked: 75 per cent of the land where the maple tree grows, on account of its rocky nature, is unsuited to the growing of grain and the farmer is therefore unwise if he does not extract from it the yearly income which is right at hand.
To-day many turn their maple groves into fuel wood. The Government should put a stop to this improvident practice. I am ready to admit that a certain income is had for the time being. Where the land may afterwards grow grain, there may be some reason for such a practice, but if not, he who commits that folly is like the man who every year encroaches on his capital, instead of investing it and living on the income. A sugar bush on a farm is more profitable than a herd of cattle which must be fed during one season in order to give returns the next. The maple bush requires neither care, nor maintenance and when its season comes, it yields its product.
I will say also that it would be wise on the farmer's part in clearing his arable land to keep, if he can, a maple bush, as the maple is valuable not only for its sugar but for its excellent lumber, which can be put to a large number of uses.
If we look back, we cannot see that anything has been done in the past to develop this natural industry. Formerly on the farm, maple sugar .and syrup were made for family use and also as a relaxation in season. It was a tradition with us to have a " sugaring " in the early spring. A very small quantity of what was turned into sugar or syrup was put up for sale. As a matter of fact, sugar and syrup were made by a moTe or less primitive process, and the prices were not..at the time such as to urge to further production by means of better equipment.
Shgar statistics locate the sugar regions in Quebec, Ontario and the Maritime provinces. Quebec accounts for about two-thirds of the production. The statistics I have referred to go as far back as 1850, and from that date to 1860, Canada pro-

duced 135 millions of pounds of maple sugar, and from 1860 to 1870, 175 millions of pounds, an advance of 40 millions of pounds; from 1870 to 1880, 190 millions, an increase of 15 millions for that decade; from 1880 to 1890, 225 millions of pounds, an increase of 35 millions, but from 1890 to 1900, we only produced 212 millions, a decrease during that decade of 13 millions. And then, from 1900 to 1910, 196 millions, a further decrease of 16 millions during that decade. I think the reason for the difference must be found in the adulteration then prevalent.
Canada's population is on the increase and so the demand for more expensive goods, and' with a sufficient protection against the falsifier there is no reason why our industry should decline instead of advancing.
To-day the situation is completely changed, maple sugar and syrup have become expensive commodities. Their market price has doubled.
Why will the sugar industry give good returns if we seriously take to it?
First, because we are now protected by law.
Secondly, because we have schools which teach and supervise the process of sugar making.
Thirdly, because, outside of local markets, we have the American market, which will be free to us after the 1st of May and two new markets in Europe, one in England and one in France. The greatest enemy of the sugar industry was adulteration. The canning of the adulterated article marks the beginning of the decline of production and it is easy to follow the increase in the process of adulteration by the decrease in the production by the farmers themselves.
At last adulterated sugar and syrup held the market. The traders sold nothing but the spurious article and with it carried on a dishonest and most harmful competition against the absolutely pure product. Every gallon of pure syrup, which was sold at 50, 60 and 75 cents had cost the producer time, labour and wood, while every gallon of the adulterated goods which was sold for the [DOT]same price had cost hardly a sigh in time and money to the falsifiers.
Such conditions became unbearable. To go' on meant the destruction of our sugar industry, I should say our national industry, because if ever an industry deserves that name, that is it, since Canada is the only country in the world that produces maple sugar and syrup. Realiz-

ing the harm being done, I, as representative of a county interested in maple sugar and syrup, decided to give the alarm by bringing the question before the Dominion Parliament. Later on, in 1912, the executive of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association took a stand and protested vigorously against the adulteration of maple products. Afterwards, petitions were sent to the ministers of Inland Revenue and of Agriculture-one. of which is noteworthy as it contained 20,000 names-requesting energetic and immediate action. But, as is always the case when a government seeks a solution which will not be prejudicial to the various interests concerned, the movement made slow though relentless progress. We have at least this to say that since last year, that industry has made giant strides, through the action of Parliament and the co-operation of the hon. minister who introduced the well-known legislation. It may be remarked that it is not enough to have a vast field to exploit, but that a market is required. To this day the local market was almost the only one. There was little exportation of sugar. For five years, Canada exported about 8,685,000 pounds of maple sugar and 20,000 gallons of syrup. Of that amount of sugar, the United States received over 99 per cent, that is 8,642,000 and about one-half the -maple syrup, while six-sevenths of the other half were exported to Great Britain. The quantity of syrup exported is insignificant, 20,000 gallons altogether during the last five years, being equivalent to 80,000 pounds of sugar which is one-fiftieth of the total weight of the exported sugar or one-thirty-fifth of its value in money. Exports, then are relatively inconsiderable, when we keep in mind that during the same time the production of sugar was about 196,000,000 pounds every year.
Therefore there need be felt no apprehension as to having a market to dispose of the sugar, since there is already a local market, and when desired there can be found as many foreign markets as are necessary because maple syrup and sugar are made only in Canada and in the New England States, -and especially because tomorrow the adulterated' product will no more bb labeled maple syrup, and a stop will be put to the dishonest competition that was carried on heretofore.
Canada offers a ready market, the consumer will be sure of giving his money in exchange for pure maple sugar and syrup.

In 1914, the hon. Mr. Caron distributed through th© railway companies nearly
25.000	samples of pure maple sugar, which turned out to be a wonderful advertisement. From all over he received letters of congratulation and the merchants received orders.
It is feared by some that'the'protection which is sought for that natural product and which is likely to be granted by the Government will result in an increase in the price and therefore in a disadvantage to the consumer. -I think there is no grounds for such fears. I rather think that the result will be to lower the prices of all the syrups that overstock the markets today and which heretofore have been sold under -the name of maple syrup and sometimes pure maple syrup. Would the consumer be better off by leaving things as they are and paying the same price for the spurious goods and the real article? Even were pure maple sugar and syrup to rise in price, when the producer has bettered them, it would be only fair to the producer. At any rate, let a stop be put to the dishonest competition carried on heretofore, and the producers will be -satisfied with present prices so long as the consumption is confined to Canada. Besides the local market, we may successfully endeavour to reach foreign lands when we shall be producing in excess of the local demand.
In 1914, on Christmas eve, Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Connaught, wife of the Governor General of Canada, had -a small box of maple sugar distributed to every Canadian soldier at the front. That gift, when it was exhibited in a large store in London, was greatly admired. The result is that orders for -several tons of sugar -have come from London, the largest city of England.
Not only England wants our sugar but there has -come an order for 45 tons or
90.000	pounds from a -single merchant in France. Lately I received from Chicago an order for 25,000 pounds of maple sugar in one-pound loaves, and the peculiar fact is that they wanted it of a rather yellow colour, as they wished to label it over -there " Golden." I answered immediately that I was neither a dealer in nor a producer of maple sugar, but I would hand over their order to one who could certainly satisfy them.
My conclusion is -that our sugar industry has a splendid outlook and if we would develop it, the Government must by all

Mr. L.AFORTUNE (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I took part in the discussion concerning this measure, when it was first introduced and enacted. At that time I congratulated the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Blondin) on what he had accomplished for the farmers.
As representative of an agricultural district where .much maple sugar and syrup is made, it is incumbent on me to see that my electors are protected to the 'fullest extent and so I concur heartily in all that has just been said by the hon. member for Vaudreuil, the apostle of th-e maple sugar industry in the province of Quebec. It is a great fraud on the public and if the statute does not go that far, I should ask the minister to make a note of my suggestion and of that of the hon. member for Vaudreuil and take the necessary measures to prevent such advertisements.

Of course, a greater protection would be secured. There is yet much room for reform along those lines.
I fully agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Vaudreuil and I insist on behalf of the country people I represent, that adequate protection should be secured against adulteration.

subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext:
Has	the
department been dbliged to prosecute any one?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext:
There was a large number of .prosecutions. Thus I see by the list before me that from 30 to 40 persons were summoned with regard to maple sugar. I must state that we prosecuted every time there was a complaint.

Air. PROUiLX (Translation): Was there a conviction in each case?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext: A number of cases are still 'pending and from the list before me I gather that there was a conviction in every case where a judgment intervened.

subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext: Has the fine been paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext: Once more I beg to call the minister's attention to the letter I have read from Calgary. His predecessor (Mr. Blondin) had stated: It is not permitted to put the word "maple" on any article which is not pure, especially an article like "mapleine." That is the kind of practice we want to stop as it is through the sale of such articles in hotels and on boats that the producers of the genuine article suffer most. I see no objection whatever to any compounded article, but let the word "maple" be taken off their labels. The Act is quite clear as to that and the ex-Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Blondin) put it quite plainly.

subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext: I believe that even to advertise it and offer it for sale is prohibited.

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext: I shall make inquiries and whenever the law can be enforced I shall deal sternly with such cases.

subtopic: W. B. MACKENZIE AND COMPANY, LIMITED.
speechtext: I would suggest, as the attendance is slim, but as some other members may wish to discuss matters arising from the estimates of the Minister of Inland Revenue, that this item be allowed to stand, with the understanding that under it 'any item in the minister's estimates may be discussed.
